steps.headline: When you look steeply up or down, the vertical edges converge too, and a third vanishing point is needed.

lead.text: A tower seen from the street, with your head tipped back to see the top, looks narrower at the top than at the bottom, although it is the same width at both. The picture plane is no longer parallel to the vertical edges, so they converge, and we need a third vanishing point for them, above the picture when we look up and below it when we look down. This is **three-point perspective**.

In the figure the first view is a level view of a tower, with two points and vertical edges. In the second view the camera is tilted up by 40°, which moves the horizon down the picture and makes the vertical edges meet at a point above. The three points are not independent: they are fixed by the direction of the viewer's gaze, which is why a picture with three points looks coherent only when the third lies on the line through the centre of the picture.

diagram.alt: A tall tower turned at an angle. Viewed level, its vertical edges stay vertical and it uses two vanishing points. Viewed from below with the camera tilted up, its vertical edges converge toward a third point above the picture.
diagram.caption: Tilting the view up adds a third vanishing point for the vertical edges.

cases.label: Looking level

steps.headline: A form pointing toward the viewer is foreshortened: its drawn length is its length times the cosine of its angle out of the picture plane.

lead.text: Hold your forearm out sideways, across your view, and it looks as long as it is. Point it straight at your eye and it looks like a stump, the hand nearly covering the elbow. This compression is **foreshortening**. In the top view of the figure, a segment lies along the picture plane at 0° and keeps its full length. As it swings toward the viewer by an angle β, its drawn length falls to its length times cos β.

For a segment of 120 units, the drawn lengths are 120 at 0°, about 92 at 40°, 60 at 60° and only about 21 at 80°. These figures use the simplest model, in which the lines of sight are treated as parallel, and perspective makes the effect stronger on a part that is close. The practical lesson is that you cannot measure a foreshortened part by its real length. Compare it with the parts beside it, as in the first lesson.

diagram.alt: A top view of a segment of length 120 swinging from lying along the picture plane toward the viewer. Its drawn length is its length times the cosine of the angle: 120 at 0 degrees, 92 at 40 degrees, 60 at 60 degrees and 21 at 80 degrees.
diagram.caption: The green bar is the length the segment has when drawn. It shrinks as the segment points more directly at the viewer. This is the parallel-projection approximation, which ignores perspective.

reveal.text: A part pointing at the viewer is compressed, and the drawing must show it that way. Drawers call this foreshortening, and it applies to arms, legs, fingers and boxes.

steps.headline: A forearm 30 cm long points 60° out of the picture plane toward the viewer. Find its drawn length.

workedSteps.text: The drawn length is the length times the cosine of the angle out of the picture plane.
The cosine of 60° is one half.

reveal.text: A box follows the rules of perspective. A forearm is a subtle form, so its drawn length is judged against the parts beside it, as in the first lesson.

lessons.orientation: Use two vanishing points, know when a third is needed, and calculate foreshortening.
lessons.nextAction: Simplify a scene into a few values and place them on a value scale.

blocks.text: Turn a box a little, so that you look at a corner of it instead of a face. The edge in front of you stays upright, and the edges on either side run away from it in opposite directions, one to the left and one to the right. Lay a ruler along the left-going ones, and they meet at a point, and the right-going ones meet at another.

The two points are the whole story of a turned box, and the same idea tells you what happens when you look up at a tower, or point a finger at your own eye. The figure shows the cube with the two directions marked in different colours.

diagram.alt: A cube turned so that no face is parallel to the picture, seen from above its top, drawn in perspective. Edges in one direction are blue and edges in the other direction are orange, and the vertical edges stay vertical. In the first view the edges are continued as dashed lines, and each colour meets at its own point on the horizon.
diagram.caption: Blue edges go to one point and orange edges to the other. Both points lie on the same horizon, and the vertical edges stay vertical.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the vanishing points a view needs, draw a box with two points, and say how much a foreshortened part is compressed.
intro.whyItMatters: Most real objects are seen at an angle, so two-point perspective covers most of the drawings you will make.

recap.keyIdea: Each direction of parallel edges that is not parallel to the picture has its own vanishing point, and a form pointing at the viewer is shortened by the cosine of its angle.

blocks.text: A box turned so that no face is parallel to the picture has horizontal edges in two directions, which meet at two points on the same horizon, while its vertical edges stay vertical. Looking steeply up or down makes the vertical edges converge as well, and gives a third point.
Points close together give a stretched view, points far apart look natural, and a form pointing at the viewer is foreshortened to its length times the cosine of its angle out of the picture plane.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson leaves line behind for a while and looks at how light and dark make a flat page look solid.

lessons.title: Value and the value scale

steps.headline: Value is how light or dark an area is, apart from its colour, and a value scale lays it out in equal steps from white to black.

lead.text: Take a coloured photograph and turn it to black and white. You lose the hues, yet the picture can still be read, because what carries its structure is how light or dark each area is. This property is called **value**, and it is separate from hue: a pale yellow and a pale blue can have the same value, and a pale yellow and a dark yellow differ only in it.

To talk about value precisely, we lay it out as a **value scale**, a row of equal steps from white to black. With five steps, each step is 100 ÷ 4 = 25 points of lightness apart, so the steps are at 100, 75, 50, 25 and 0 percent. With nine steps the gap is 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 points. Scales for painters are made so that neighbouring steps *look* evenly spaced, because the eye notices differences among darks more easily than among lights, and a scale of equal amounts of reflected light would not look even.

afterFigure.text: The shades in the figure are the ones the page provides, so a nine-step scale shares some of them between neighbours. Read the numbers for the true spacing.

diagram.alt: A scale of grey squares from white to black. The first view has five steps labelled 100, 75, 50, 25 and 0 percent light. The second has nine steps spaced 12.5 points apart.
diagram.caption: Equal steps from white to black. Five steps are 25 points apart, and nine steps are 12.5 points apart.

steps.headline: A picture reads clearly when its values are grouped into a few masses, and three to five are enough.

lead.text: Squint at a scene until the detail dissolves, and what is left is a few large patches of light and dark. The figure shows a tree both ways. The first drawing outlines every leaf, and the second has only a pale sky, a light grey ground, a darker mass of foliage and a nearly black trunk, and yet it reads as a tree at once. Reducing a scene to a few values like this is called **simplifying**, and three to five masses is usually the right number.

The habit works because the eye reads shape from boundaries between values. A mass that is clearly lighter or darker than its neighbours makes a clear shape, while two similar values blur into one. Decide the values of the large masses first, as we decided the large shapes first in the opening lesson, and add detail only inside the masses.

diagram.alt: A tree on a hill drawn two ways. In the first every leaf and branch is outlined. In the second the scene is reduced to a handful of flat masses: a light sky, a light grey ground, a darker round mass of foliage and a nearly black trunk.
diagram.caption: The second drawing has no detail and still reads as a tree, because its values are arranged correctly.

steps.headline: Local value is an object's own lightness, and light then makes each face lighter or darker than it.

lead.text: A white cube and a black cube have different **local values**: this is the lightness each has under even light. Put them in a room with a lamp above, and the top of each is brighter than its sides. The values we see are the local value changed by the light, and the figure shows that the shaded side of the white cube can end up about as dark as the lit top of the black one.

This is why you should not copy local values from memory. A white shirt in shadow is mid-grey and a black coat in sun is dim, and a drawing that makes the shirt white and the coat black will look flat. Judge each patch by the value you *see*, comparing it with the patches beside it as we did with lengths, and keep the local value in mind only as a reason for the pattern.

diagram.alt: Two cubes, one pale and one dark. The first view shows each as a single flat value, its local value. The second view shows them lit from above: the pale cube has a bright top and a mid-grey shaded side, and the dark cube has a mid-grey top and a nearly black side.
diagram.caption: The pale cube in shade and the dark cube in light end up with similar values, so lighting can hide local value.

reveal.text: The values you see are the local value changed by the light. A white shirt in shadow is mid-grey, and drawing it white ignores the light.
Green is the lightest, and the next screen gives the weights behind it.

steps.headline: Screens convert colour to grey with weights of 0.2126 for red, 0.7152 for green and 0.0722 for blue, so green is far lighter than blue.

lead.text: Computers need a rule for turning a colour into one grey value, and the rule used for HD video, from Recommendation BT.709 of the International Telecommunication Union, is **luma** = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, where R, G and B run from 0 to 255 on a screen. The weights add up to 1, so white (255, 255, 255) stays at 255, and they reflect the eye's different sensitivity to the three colours of light.

Apply it to the pure colours. Red gives 0.2126 × 255 ≈ 54, green gives 0.7152 × 255 ≈ 182 and blue gives 0.0722 × 255 ≈ 18, as in the figure. This is a standard approximation of how light a colour looks, worked out on gamma-encoded screen values, and it is not a physical measurement of light. It still explains an observation that every painter makes sooner or later: a pure blue and a pure red look alike in a grey photograph, both dark, and a pure green looks much lighter.

afterFigure.text: The same idea guides drawings of coloured subjects: when you convert hues to pencil, decide how light each one is, rather than copying its brightness as the colour seems.

diagram.alt: Two bar charts. The first shows the three Rec. 709 luma weights, 0.2126 for red, 0.7152 for green and 0.0722 for blue, which add up to 1. The second shows the grey each pure colour becomes out of 255: red 54, green 182 and blue 18.
diagram.caption: Green carries most of the lightness and blue carries least. The grey levels are the weights times 255, rounded.

steps.headline: Find the grey level of the colour (R 200, G 100, B 50).

workedSteps.text: Multiply each channel by its weight.
The green channel contributes the larger part of the grey, even though its value is only 100.
Blue adds only a little.
The grey level is the sum of the three contributions, rounded to the nearest whole number.

reveal.text: Red adds about 54 and green about 182, so yellow comes to 237 out of 255, almost as light as white.
A change of hue does not separate two areas in pencil. A difference of value does, and it is what carries the structure of the picture.

lessons.orientation: Place values on a scale, simplify a scene to a few masses, and convert a colour to grey.
lessons.nextAction: Model a form with a lit side, a core shadow and a cast shadow, and calculate shadow length.

blocks.text: Squint at the room you're in until the detail dissolves. What is left is not colours, and not outlines. It is a few large patches of light and dark, the window bright, the wall mid, the furniture darker, and you could draw them as flat shapes and still be understood.

Those patches are the values of the scene, and they carry the structure of a picture more than anything else does. The figure shows a tree with every leaf drawn and the same tree as four flat masses, and the second is the one that reads better.

diagram.alt: A tree on a hill drawn two ways. In the first every leaf and branch is outlined. In the second the scene is reduced to a handful of flat masses: a light sky, a light grey ground, a darker round mass of foliage and a nearly black trunk.
diagram.caption: The second drawing has no detail and still reads as a tree, because its values are arranged correctly.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a value on a scale, group a scene into a few masses, and convert a colour to a grey level with the luma weights.
intro.whyItMatters: Value is what makes a drawing look solid, and a good value pattern survives any amount of missing detail.

recap.keyIdea: Value is lightness apart from hue, and a few well-placed values carry a picture.

blocks.text: Value is how light or dark an area is, and a value scale divides it into equal steps, 25 points apart for five steps and 12.5 for nine. A scene reads best when grouped into three to five masses, and the value you see combines an object's local value with the effect of light.
To turn a colour into a grey level we use luma, 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B for screens, which makes green much lighter than red and blue.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows how light creates the values on a single form, from the lit side to the shadow it casts.

lessons.title: Light and form

reveal.text: The shadow falls to the lower right, away from the light. The next screen names the parts of the light on the sphere itself.

steps.headline: On a lit sphere the values run from highlight through light and halftone to a core shadow, with reflected light at the edge.

lead.text: The figure shows a sphere lit from the upper left, drawn as flat bands. The brightest small spot, where the surface faces the light most directly, is the **highlight**. Around it are the **light** and the **halftone**, which grow darker as the surface turns away. The line where the surface turns from light into shadow is the **terminator**, and it is drawn as a curve around the sphere, since the sphere is round.

Just inside the terminator, on the shadow side, is the **core shadow**, the darkest band on the form. It is not at the outer edge, which is a common mistake. Light bounces off the table and the walls and strikes the shadow side from below, so a strip of **reflected light** lifts the edge, and the darkest value sits between the terminator and that strip. Reflected light is never as bright as the lit side, and a drawing that makes it too bright makes the form look flat.

afterFigure.text: The order, from the light to the dark, is highlight, light, halftone, terminator, core shadow, reflected light. The five bands in the figure use only the five shades of the page's palette, so the real transitions on a form are softer.

diagram.alt: A sphere lit from the upper left, drawn in flat bands of value from lightest to darkest. The first view labels them: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow and reflected light, plus a cast shadow on the ground to the lower right. The second view adds an arrow for the light and an arrow for the direction the shadow falls.
diagram.caption: The darkest band, the core shadow, lies just inside the edge on the side away from the light. A thin strip of reflected light lifts the edge itself.

reveal.text: Reflected light lifts the edge of the shadow side but stays darker than the lit side. A drawing that makes it too bright loses the core shadow and the form looks flat.

steps.headline: A cast shadow falls on the surface behind an object, away from the light, and is darkest where it touches the object.

lead.text: The shadow a form throws onto the ground is its **cast shadow**, and the rule from the opening question is that it falls on the side away from the light, along the line from the light through the object. With the light at the upper left, the shadow goes to the lower right, as in the second view of the figure. Moving the light changes the shadow at once: light from the right puts it on the left, and light from behind the object puts it toward you.

Near the object the shadow is darkest, because the object blocks almost all the light there and little is reflected into it. Farther away the shadow lightens and its edge softens. Draw the shadow with its darkest value where it meets the object, called the contact shadow, and make it lighter with distance, and the object will look as if it sits on the surface instead of floating above it.

diagram.alt: The same sphere with an arrow for the light coming from the upper left and an arrow below pointing to the lower right, the direction the shadow falls.
diagram.caption: The shadow falls on the side opposite the light.

reveal.text: A shadow is darkest where it meets the object, and it lightens with distance. That contact shadow is what makes an object sit on the surface and not float above it.

steps.headline: The shadow of a vertical object of height h is h ÷ tan a long, where a is the angle of the sun above the horizon.

lead.text: Shadows are not just a direction, since their length is also set by the light. In the figure a 2 m post stands in sunlight. A ray from the sun passes over the top of the post and lands on the tip of the shadow, and with the sun at an angle *a* above the horizon, the post and its shadow make a right triangle whose angle at the shadow's tip is *a*. The tangent of that angle is the height divided by the shadow, so **shadow length = h ÷ tan a**.

Try the three sun heights. At 30° the shadow is 2 ÷ tan 30° = 3.46 m, at 45° it is exactly 2 m, because tan 45° = 1, and at 60° it is 1.15 m. A longer shadow therefore means a *lower* sun, near sunrise or sunset, and not a brighter one. The rule is for a vertical post on level ground, and it assumes the sun's rays are parallel, which is accurate enough for the sun.

afterFigure.text: A drawing shows the time of day through its shadows: long ones mean low sun, short ones mean the sun is high.

diagram.alt: A 2 metre post and its shadow on level ground for three sun heights. At 30 degrees above the horizon the shadow is 3.46 metres, at 45 degrees it is 2 metres, and at 60 degrees it is 1.15 metres. A dashed ray runs from the sun over the top of the post to the tip of the shadow.
diagram.caption: The same 2 m post at three sun heights, drawn at 60 units per metre. The lower the sun, the longer the shadow.

reveal.text: At 45° a shadow is as long as the object, so a longer shadow means a lower sun. Taller objects cast longer shadows at the same sun height.

steps.headline: Find the shadow of a child 1.5 m tall when the sun is 30° above the horizon.

workedSteps.text: The shadow is the height divided by the tangent of the sun's angle.
The tangent of 30° is about 0.5774.
The shadow length is wanted in metres, to two decimal places.

reveal.text: Shadow is what shows form, and its grading is what makes the sphere round. The terminator and the core shadow are the places where that grading is easiest to get wrong.
The sun's rays are parallel, so identical posts on level ground have shadows of the same length. A long shadow belongs to a low sun, and every shadow in the scene shares it.

lessons.orientation: Name the bands of light on a form, place a cast shadow, and calculate shadow length.
lessons.nextAction: Control edges and build tone with hatching, and count how much of the paper a hatching covers.

blocks.text: Hold a ball under a lamp and look at it. The side facing the lamp is bright, the far side is dark, and you might expect the darkest place to be the very edge of the ball, where it turns away from you. It isn't. A little way in from the edge there is a band darker than the edge itself, and the edge is lifted by light bouncing back from the table.

The ball also throws a shadow, which has a direction and a length that are both fixed by where the light is. The figure shows the bands on a sphere lit from the upper left, with the shadow on the table.

diagram.alt: A sphere lit from the upper left, drawn in flat bands of value from lightest to darkest. The first view labels them: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow and reflected light, plus a cast shadow on the ground to the lower right. The second view adds an arrow for the light and an arrow for the direction the shadow falls.
diagram.caption: The darkest band, the core shadow, lies just inside the edge on the side away from the light. A thin strip of reflected light lifts the edge itself.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the bands of light on a form, say where a cast shadow falls, and calculate its length from the sun's angle.
intro.whyItMatters: Light is what makes a drawn form look solid, and its rules can be worked out rather than guessed.

recap.keyIdea: Light makes bands on a form, with the core shadow just inside the terminator, and a cast shadow falls away from the light with a length of height divided by tan of the sun's angle.

blocks.text: On a form lit from one side the values run from the highlight through the light and halftone to the terminator, then the core shadow, with reflected light lifting the edge. The cast shadow falls away from the light and is darkest where it touches the object.
For a vertical object on level ground the shadow is its height divided by the tangent of the sun's angle, so a low sun means a long shadow.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at edges, and at hatching, the marks that build the values you have just placed.

lessons.title: Edges and rendering

steps.headline: A hard edge is a sharp change in value, a soft edge a gradual one, and a lost edge fades into the background.

lead.text: The edge of a form is where its value changes, and it can change in three ways. In the first view of the figure, marker 1 is a **hard edge**, where the lit side meets the dark background and the value jumps at once. Marker 2 is a **soft edge**, the turn into shadow, where the value changes gradually over a distance. Marker 3 is a **lost edge**: the sphere's shadow side has the same value as the background, so the boundary vanishes and the eye completes it.

The second view shows what happens when we draw every edge hard. The sphere looks cut out of paper, because nothing about it is turning or sitting in air. A mixture of the three kinds is what makes a form look round and set in space, and it also leads the eye: we look at hard edges first, and a lost edge lets a shape dissolve into its surroundings.

afterFigure.text: Choose the edge from the values on each side of it, instead of from an outline. Where the two values are far apart, the edge is hard, and where they are equal, it is lost.

diagram.alt: A sphere lit from the left against a dark background. In the first view its lit edge on the left is sharp, the transition at the terminator is gradual, and its shadow side on the right has the same value as the background so the edge disappears. Three markers number these. In the second view every edge is outlined in a hard line and the sphere looks like a cut-out.
diagram.caption: Marker 1 is where the lit side meets the dark background, marker 2 is the turn into shadow, and marker 3 is where the shadow side meets a background of the same value.

reveal.text: The values 10 and 90 are far apart, so the change at the boundary is sudden, which makes a hard edge. Where the values match, the edge would be lost.

lead.text: Hatching is a set of parallel lines, and the tone it makes depends on how much of the paper the lines cover.

reveal.text: The close patch is darker, because its lines leave less bare paper. The next screen gives the rule: the share covered is the line width divided by the spacing.

steps.headline: Hatching builds tone from parallel lines, and the share of paper they cover is the line width divided by the spacing.

lead.text: **Hatching** is a set of parallel lines, and it makes tone by leaving some of the paper bare. Each repeat of the pattern has one line and one gap, so the **coverage** is the width of the line divided by the spacing from one line to the next. In the first view of the figure, stripes 2 units wide at a spacing of 10 cover 2 ÷ 10 = 20 percent, those at 5 cover 40 percent, and those at 20 cover 10 percent.

So a drawer has two ways to darken a hatched area: draw the lines closer together, or draw them thicker with more pressure. Close spacing is the cleaner way, since the line width stays the same and the tone changes in predictable steps. From a normal reading distance the eye cannot separate the lines, and merges them into a tone of the grey that the coverage implies.

diagram.alt: Hatching swatches built from stripes of exact width. The first view shows three squares with stripes 2 units wide spaced 5, 10 and 20 units apart, covering 40, 20 and 10 percent. The second shows one layer at 10 apart covering 20 percent and the same layer crossed by a second at right angles, covering 36 percent.
diagram.caption: Stripes are drawn as rectangles, so each swatch's coverage is the stripe width divided by the spacing, and a crossed pair covers 1 − 0.8 × 0.8 = 36 percent.

reveal.text: Closer spacing keeps the line width and raises the coverage. Halving the spacing doubles the share of paper covered.

steps.headline: Cross-hatching lays a second set of lines across the first, and each layer covers a share of the paper that is still bare.

lead.text: To go darker than one layer allows, we lay a second set of lines at an angle across the first, which is **cross-hatching**. If one layer covers 20 percent, then 80 percent is bare, and a second layer, drawn independently, covers 20 percent of *that*. The paper left bare is 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, and so the covered share is 1 − 0.64 = 0.36, or 36 percent, as in the second view of the figure.

The lesson of the arithmetic is that layers do not simply add: two layers of 20 percent give 36 percent, not 40. Each extra layer gives a smaller gain, which is why it is easier to deepen a midtone with layers than to reach black with them. The rule is 1 − (1 − c)ⁿ for n layers of coverage c, as in the second figure.

afterFigure.text: Draw the second layer at an angle to the first, since a layer that runs the same way only packs the lines closer together, while a layer at an angle crosses every gap and darkens the patch evenly.

reveal.text: The bare paper is 0.75 × 0.75 = 0.5625, so the covered share is 1 − 0.5625 = 0.4375, which is 43.75 percent.

steps.headline: Find how much paper is covered by two crossed layers of hatching that each cover 10 percent.

workedSteps.text: One layer covers 10 percent, so it leaves 90 percent of the paper bare.
The second layer leaves 90 percent of what the first left bare, so the bare share is the product.
The covered share is what is not left bare.

steps.headline: Hard H pencils make light marks and soft B pencils make dark ones, and darker tone is better made by layers than by pressure.

lead.text: Pencils are graded by how hard the lead is. H pencils have hard leads that leave light, fine marks, B pencils have soft leads that leave dark, broad ones, and HB sits in the middle. The numbers say how far each way: 2H is harder than H, and 6B is far softer than 2B. The scale in the figure runs from 4H to 6B.

A common belief is that you make a darker tone by pressing harder. Pressing hard crushes the paper's surface and shines it, and it makes the tone difficult to adjust. It is better to reach a dark tone with a softer pencil or with more layers, since each layer adds coverage as the arithmetic of crossing showed. In the same way, rubbing a tone with a finger smooths it but removes the texture and the edges, so it is a choice and not a rendering technique.

The size of the light sets how soft the shadow edge is, so the edge is chosen from the light and the values together.

lessons.orientation: Choose edge types, calculate hatching coverage, and build tone with layers.
lessons.nextAction: Describe colour by hue, value and chroma, and work out complements in paint and in light.

blocks.text: Look at the edge of a face against a dark wall. Along the jaw the line is crisp, at the cheek it melts gradually from light into shade, and where the hair meets the shadow behind it, the edge is simply gone. A drawing that treats all three the same, with one confident outline, looks like a cut-out.

The tone itself is made of marks, and a drawer can work out how much of the paper a set of lines will cover. The figure shows the sphere both ways, with a mixture of edges and with every edge made hard.

diagram.alt: A sphere lit from the left against a dark background. In the first view its lit edge on the left is sharp, the transition at the terminator is gradual, and its shadow side on the right has the same value as the background so the edge disappears. Three markers number these. In the second view every edge is outlined in a hard line and the sphere looks like a cut-out.
diagram.caption: Marker 1 is where the lit side meets the dark background, marker 2 is the turn into shadow, and marker 3 is where the shadow side meets a background of the same value.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the three kinds of edge, work out how much paper a hatching covers, and build a darker tone with layers.
intro.whyItMatters: Edges and tone are what turn outlines into forms, and the arithmetic of coverage makes tones repeatable.

recap.keyIdea: Edges vary from hard to lost, and hatching covers its line width divided by its spacing, with layers adding less each time.

blocks.text: An edge may be hard, soft or lost, depending on how quickly the value changes across it, and a drawing with all three looks round and set in air. Hatching covers the width of its lines divided by their spacing, and a second layer covers a share of what the first left bare, so two layers of 20 percent cover 36 percent, not 40.
Softer pencils and more layers darken a tone more cleanly than pressure does.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson brings colour in, describing it by hue, value and chroma, and looking at which colours sit opposite each other.

lessons.title: Colour theory

steps.headline: Every colour has a hue, a value and a chroma, and we can describe any patch by giving all three.

lead.text: Suppose you want to tell someone about a colour you can see, a patch of dull orange-brown on a wall. The first thing to give is its **hue**, the family it belongs to, which here is orange, and the wheel in the figure shows twelve hues in order, from red round through orange, yellow, green and blue to violet and back. The second is its **value**, how light or dark it is, which we met in the lesson on value. The third is its **chroma**, how pure or strong the colour is, running from grey, which has none, to the most vivid colour of that hue.

Albert Munsell, an American painter and teacher, built his system of colour notation on these three attributes, and artists still use them. They are independent: a pale and a dark orange share a hue and differ in value, and a vivid and a dull orange share a hue and differ in chroma. A common slip is to treat colours of the same brightness as if they had the same hue, when the two properties are separate.

afterFigure.text: A drawing in pencil has value and no hue or chroma, and a painting must settle all three, which is why this lesson separates them.

diagram.alt: A ring of twelve hue names, from red at the top clockwise through orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. In the second view, a line joins each hue to the one directly opposite: red to green, red-orange to blue-green, orange to blue, yellow-orange to blue-violet, yellow to violet and yellow-green to red-violet.
diagram.caption: The twelve hues of the traditional painter's wheel. Each complement lies directly across the ring, six places round.

reveal.text: Chroma is separate from hue and from value, so two oranges can share both and still differ in how vivid they are. Mixing in a little of the complement lowers chroma without changing hue.

steps.headline: Light mixes by adding red, green and blue, and pigment mixes by subtracting cyan, magenta and yellow.

lead.text: The rules for mixing depend on what is being mixed. A screen makes colour by *adding* light, and its primaries are red, green and blue: red and green light together make yellow, green and blue make cyan, red and blue make magenta, and all three together make white. This is **additive mixing**. Paint and ink work the other way. Each pigment absorbs part of the light that falls on it, so mixing pigments takes light away, and the primaries are cyan, magenta and yellow: cyan and yellow together make green, since cyan absorbs red and yellow absorbs blue, and all three make something near black. This is **subtractive mixing**.

You may have been taught that red, yellow and blue are the primary colours of all mixing. That set works for traditional paint, and it is the one behind the painter's wheel we use later, but it is not true of light, and printers use cyan, magenta and yellow instead. The primaries belong to the system, not to colour itself.

diagram.alt: Three overlapping circles. For light, the circles are red, green and blue; where red and green overlap the result is yellow, green and blue give cyan, red and blue give magenta, and all three give white. For pigment, the circles are cyan, yellow and magenta; cyan with yellow gives green, yellow with magenta gives red, magenta with cyan gives blue, and all three give a dark, near-black mix.
diagram.caption: Light mixes by adding and pigment by taking away. In each view the labels name the colours in the overlaps.

steps.headline: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on a wheel, and on a screen the complement of a colour is found by subtracting each channel from 255.

lead.text: Two colours are **complements** if they sit directly opposite each other on a wheel. On the traditional painter's wheel, red is opposite green, blue is opposite orange, and yellow is opposite violet, as the second view of the figure shows. Mixed in paint, complements give a dull neutral, and placed side by side they make each other look stronger.

On a screen we can be exact. If a colour has red, green and blue channels (R, G, B) out of 255, its complement is (255 − R, 255 − G, 255 − B). The complement of orange (255, 128, 0) is (0, 127, 255), a blue, and the complement of pure red (255, 0, 0) is (0, 255, 255), cyan. Notice that the screen's complement of red is cyan, and the painter's is green. Each is correct for its own wheel, and the sum of a colour and its screen complement is white, since each channel adds to 255.

diagram.alt: A ring of twelve hue names, from red at the top clockwise through orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. In the second view, a line joins each hue to the one directly opposite: red to green, red-orange to blue-green, orange to blue, yellow-orange to blue-violet, yellow to violet and yellow-green to red-violet.
diagram.caption: The twelve hues of the traditional painter's wheel. Each complement lies directly across the ring, six places round.

reveal.text: The screen complement is found by subtracting each channel from 255, and the painter's wheel is built on mixing pigment. Each answer is correct for its own system.
Yellow is opposite violet, and a colour mixed with its opposite loses chroma, so a little yellow dulls the violet.

steps.headline: Find the screen complement of the colour (30, 144, 255), a bright blue.

workedSteps.text: Subtract the red channel from 255.
The green channel of the colour is 144.
Subtract the blue channel from 255.
The complement is (225, 111, 0), an orange. Adding it to the original, channel by channel, gives 255 in every channel, which is white.

steps.headline: Reds, oranges and yellows are warm, and blues and greens are cool, but warm and cool are relative to the neighbours.

lead.text: Painters call the colours around red, orange and yellow *warm* and those around blue and green *cool*, and use the contrast to show light. In a landscape, sunlit ground is often drawn warm and the shadows cool. This is **colour temperature**, and it is a separate matter from the physical temperature of anything.

The labels are not fixed. A green that leans toward yellow is warm beside a blue-green, and the same green is cool beside an orange. The figure shows the same green patch beside orange and beside blue. We can say only that one colour is warmer or cooler *than another*, which is why drawers judge temperature by comparing neighbours, as they judge length and value.

diagram.alt: The same green patch twice, once beside an orange patch and once beside a blue patch. Next to orange it reads as the cooler of the two, and next to blue it reads as the warmer.
diagram.caption: Warm and cool are relative: a colour is warm or cool compared with what is beside it.

steps.headline: A colour looks different beside another colour, because the eye exaggerates the difference between neighbours.

lead.text: Place the same grey patch on four tinted backgrounds, as in the figure, and the patches do not look alike. Each tends to look slightly tinted toward the complement of its background, and a patch on a stronger background can also look lighter or darker. The effect is called **simultaneous contrast**, and the French chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul, who worked at the Gobelins tapestry factory, described it in 1839 after complaints that dyed threads looked different beside one another.

The second view proves the patches are the same, since a single strip of grey crosses all four backgrounds, and the effect is weaker when the neighbours are joined. For a drawer this means that a colour is never judged alone. A colour mixed on the palette and put on the paper beside others will look different, and a dull colour beside its complement looks stronger.

afterFigure.text: The effect is the reason to use the complement deliberately, to make a small area of a colour glow beside its opposite.

diagram.alt: A grey patch of one value placed on four tinted backgrounds, blue, orange, green and red. The second view shows a single grey strip running across all four backgrounds, with no gaps.
diagram.caption: The grey is the same in every patch. Compare how it seems on each ground, then see the strip that joins them.

A colour beside its complement looks stronger, so a small patch of orange among blue glows. The same pair mixed together would give a dull neutral.

lessons.orientation: Describe colour by hue, value and chroma, and find complements and temperature.
lessons.nextAction: Plan a picture with thumbnails, a focal point, thirds and leading lines.

blocks.text: Try to describe the colour of a brick wall to someone who cannot see it. Saying it is red is not enough, since it might be a bright red or a dull one, a pale one or a dark one. You need three separate pieces of information, and the three are the same ones every painter has used to talk about colour: which family it belongs to, how light it is, and how strong it is.

Those three are called hue, value and chroma. The figure shows two of them as scales, and the wheel of hues comes next. Once you can separate them, a lot of confusing advice about colour becomes simple.

diagram.alt: Left, a stack of five squares from white at the top to black at the bottom, labelled value from 10 down to 0. Right, three squares of one blue hue at increasing chroma, from grey through a weak blue to a strong blue.
diagram.caption: Value runs from dark to light and chroma from grey to strong. Hue is the family of the colour, and it is described in words.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to describe a colour by hue, value and chroma, tell light from pigment mixing, and find a colour's complement.
intro.whyItMatters: Colour is easier to control once its three attributes are separated, and complements give a reliable way of making colours strong or dull.

recap.keyIdea: A colour is described by hue, value and chroma, and its complement lies opposite it, found on a screen by subtracting each channel from 255.

blocks.text: We describe any colour by its hue, its value and its chroma, and the three can be changed independently. Light mixes by adding red, green and blue, pigment mixes by subtracting cyan, magenta and yellow, and the traditional painter's wheel has its own complements: red with green, blue with orange, yellow with violet.
On a screen the complement is found by subtracting each channel from 255. Warm and cool are relative, and simultaneous contrast changes how a colour looks beside others.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson arranges everything so far into a picture, starting from small thumbnails and a point of focus.

lessons.title: Composition

lead.text: Many painters divide a picture into thirds across and down, and place the main subject where the lines cross.

reveal.text: Centred, the tree is calm and static, and half the picture on each side does little. The next screens use the thirds as a way to move it, after we look at where compositions begin.

steps.headline: A thumbnail is a small, quick sketch used to test arrangements, because the first arrangement you think of is rarely the best.

lead.text: The decisions that make a picture work are mostly made before the drawing begins, and the cheapest way to make them is a **thumbnail**: a sketch a few centimetres across, drawn in a few minutes, with only the big shapes and values. In the figure, six thumbnails of one tree and one horizon arrange the same two things six different ways, and they do not all work equally well. The tree centred in a frame with the horizon at half height is calm and static, and the one in the corner is awkward.

Why six, and not one? The first idea is the one you already had in your head, and it gets better by comparison. If you draw six, you can pick the one with the clearest focal point and use the others to learn from. Skipping thumbnails is the usual way to start a large drawing with a weak arrangement and only find out when it is finished.

afterFigure.text: Keep them small and fast, since a thumbnail that takes half an hour has become a drawing, and you will be unwilling to throw it away.

The second view enlarges number 2 with dashed thirds lines showing the tree on a vertical third and the horizon on a horizontal third.

steps.headline: The focal point is where the picture is read first, and the rule of thirds suggests placing it near one of four intersections.

lead.text: Every picture needs a place that the eye is meant to read first, which is its **focal point**. A drawer makes it by contrast, by detail, by the colour that differs from the rest, and by position. A common choice of position comes from the **rule of thirds**: divide the picture into thirds both ways, and put the focal point near one of the four places where the lines cross. In a picture 900 units wide and 600 tall, the vertical lines are at x = 300 and 600, the horizontal ones at y = 200 and 400, and the intersections are (300, 200), (600, 200), (300, 400) and (600, 400).

Is it a law? No. John Thomas Smith described a version of it in a book on landscape in 1797, and it has lasted because it avoids the two commonest faults: a subject in the exact centre, which is static and wastes half the picture on either side, and a subject jammed against an edge. Treat the thirds as a first guess, and move away from them when a thumbnail tells you to.

afterFigure.text: The second view of the figure shows another division, the golden section, which comes next.

reveal.text: The lines are at one third and two thirds across and down, and where they cross are the four places to try the focal point. The coordinate is measured down from the top, as it is on a screen.

steps.headline: The golden section divides a length so that the whole is to the larger part as the larger part is to the smaller, giving 1 to 1.618.

lead.text: There is another traditional division, the **golden section**, in which a length is cut so that the whole is to the larger part as the larger part is to the smaller. The ratio is about 1.618, and for a width of 1000 units the larger part is 1000 ÷ 1.618 ≈ 618 and the smaller part is 1000 − 618 = 382, as in the second view of the figure. The golden lines lie slightly closer to the middle than the thirds, which would be at 333 and 667.

The golden section has a long history in writing about art, but it deserves a cool head. The difference between 333 and 382 is small and the eye cannot tell, so there is no evidence that one is better than the other. It is a useful second guess for a grid, and like the thirds it is a starting point and not a requirement.

steps.headline: Lines in a picture can lead the eye along a path toward the focal point, and the weights of the shapes should be balanced.

lead.text: The eye travels along lines, which makes them a way of directing a viewer. A road, a river, a fence or the edge of a shadow that runs toward the focal point is a **leading line**. In the figure a house sits at the upper-right intersection, and in the second view a road from the lower-left corner carries the eye up to it. Without the road the house is a small spot that is easy to miss.

The second matter is balance. Shapes have **visual weight**, which depends on size but also on value, colour and detail: a small dark shape weighs more than a pale one of the same size. A picture is balanced when its weights are spread so that it does not seem to tip, and a large pale shape on one side can balance a small dark one placed far from the centre on the other. Symmetry is one way to balance, but a picture that is balanced without being symmetrical looks livelier.

afterFigure.text: The second figure on this screen shows balance: the first view is dark on one side only, and the second balances a large pale square with a small dark one far to the right.

diagram.alt: A frame with a small house at the upper-right third intersection. In the first view nothing else is drawn. In the second a road runs from the lower-left corner up to the house, with an arrow along it showing the path of the eye. Two more views show balance: one with all the dark weight on the left, and one in which a large pale square is balanced by a small dark one on the right.

reveal.text: Roads, rivers, fences, shadows and rows of trees can all do the same job. Each is a leading line when it runs toward the focal point.
A starting point is the right description: the rule helps in most cases, and good pictures break it deliberately.

steps.headline: Plan a picture from six thumbnails at five minutes each.

workedSteps.text: Choose the subject, and draw six small frames in your sketchbook with the same proportions as the final picture.
Draw each thumbnail in five minutes, using only three or four values and placing the focal point differently each time.
Choose the one with the clearest focal point, and write one sentence on why it works, such as which leading line or balance it uses.

reveal.text: Balance depends on visual weight, which comes from value, colour and detail as well as size. A small dark shape far from the centre can balance a large pale one.

lessons.orientation: Plan a picture with thumbnails, thirds, leading lines and balance.
lessons.nextAction: Run a whole study from thumbnail to finish, and judge it against clear criteria.

blocks.text: Imagine a single tree on a hill. Draw it in the middle of the page with the horizon cutting the frame in half, and it looks calm and slightly dead. Move the tree a third of the way in from the left and drop the horizon to the lower third, and the same tree has room to look out across the page.
Nothing in the drawing skill changed, only the arrangement. Artists settle arrangements in small sketches made before the real drawing, and the figure shows six such sketches of the same two things.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to plan a picture with thumbnails, place a focal point using thirds, and use leading lines and balance.
intro.whyItMatters: A good arrangement makes a modest drawing read well, and a poor one spoils a careful drawing.

recap.keyIdea: Settle the arrangement in thumbnails first, and use thirds, leading lines and balance as starting points.

blocks.text: A thumbnail is a small, quick sketch that tests an arrangement, and six of them are cheaper than one failed drawing. The rule of thirds puts a focal point near one of four intersections, such as (300, 200) in a 900 by 600 frame, and the golden section divides a width of 1000 at 382 and 618.
Leading lines carry the eye to the focal point, and balance spreads visual weight so that a large pale shape can balance a small dark one.

recap.nextHook: The final lesson puts everything together in one complete study, with a time plan and a way of judging the result.

lessons.title: A complete study

steps.headline: A study goes from large to small: placement, large shapes, values, edges and then the final check.

lead.text: The figure follows a still life of a mug and an apple through five stages, and the order is the point. First you plan, with thumbnails and boxes that say where each object goes. Then you **block in** the large shapes and their proportions lightly, using the sighting and ratios from the third lesson. Then you lay in the values as a few flat masses, then work the edges, hard where they should be hard and lost where the shadow merges, and last you check the whole from a distance.

Each stage assumes the one before is right. That is why details come last. A finished eye drawn in the wrong place has to be rubbed out along with the rest of the face, so the work is wasted, whereas an error in the block-in costs a few light lines. Starting with the details is the commonest reason that a drawing takes too long.

afterFigure.text: The order is also a kind of attention. Early stages look at the whole picture and late stages look at small parts, and a drawing in which the attention runs the wrong way tends to lose the whole.

diagram.alt: A still life of a mug and an apple at five stages. First, dashed boxes mark where each object goes. Second, light outlines give the large shapes. Third, flat masses of three values are filled in. Fourth, edges are drawn hard, soft and lost. Fifth, the finished study with a note to step back and compare.

reveal.text: A finished detail in the wrong place has to be rubbed out along with the rest, so large decisions come first and details last. The values stage comes before the edges, since an edge is a change in value.

steps.headline: A fixed time is divided so that the large decisions get the most time, and a typical split is 10, 20, 40, 20 and 10 percent.

lead.text: Time is the other thing to plan. A common split gives 10 percent to planning, 20 percent to the block-in, 40 percent to the values, 20 percent to the edges and 10 percent to the final check. In a one-hour study that is 6, 12, 24, 12 and 6 minutes, and in the half-hour version in the figure it is 3, 6, 12, 6 and 3. Each stage is a percentage of the total, so the same plan scales to any length.

The values get the biggest share because they do most to make the study look solid, as the lesson on value showed. These percentages are a teaching convention and not a law of drawing: if you know that you fix proportions slowly, you might give the block-in more. The useful habit is to decide the split before you begin, and to move on when a stage's time has run out, since a stage left unfinished can be corrected in the next.

reveal.text: Edges get about a fifth of the time, and values get the biggest share. When a stage's time has run out, the next stage is the place to put right what was left.

steps.headline: Split a 45-minute study with the same percentages: 10, 20, 40, 20 and 10.

workedSteps.text: Planning and the final check each take 10 percent of the time.
The block-in and the edges each take 20 percent.
The values take 40 percent of the time.
The five stages should add up to the 45 minutes of the study.

steps.headline: Looking at a drawing from a distance, or in a mirror, shows errors in proportion and value that closeness hides.

lead.text: When you are close to a drawing you see its marks, and when you are far you see its shapes. Errors of proportion and value are errors of shapes, so they show up from a distance. This is the rule of the depth-cues lesson at work: the apparent size of a thing is inversely proportional to its distance, so a drawing 0.5 m from your eyes looks four times as big as one viewed from 2 m, and from 2 m a small error in a mass looks as small as a pencil mark does close up, while the whole composition becomes visible.

Two other ways of looking give the same help. A mirror shows your drawing reversed, and the reversed picture looks new, so a fault in the balance or in a proportion often leaps out. A photo of the drawing on a phone, viewed small or in greyscale, does the same for value. Do it at the end of each stage, and treat a mistake you find as a cheap one, since you found it before the next stage was built on it.

afterFigure.text: The habit is to alternate: draw close, step back, then draw close again. A drawing that is only ever seen close up has only been half looked at.

reveal.text: From a distance the whole drawing is smaller and its shapes show, so errors of proportion and value stand out. Alternating between close and far is the habit.

steps.headline: A self-review scores a study on proportion, value structure, form, edges, composition and process, and the lowest score is what to practise next.

lead.text: A study should end with a judgement, and a judgement needs criteria set before you look. Six cover most of what this course has taught. **Proportion**: are the shapes and the ratios between them right? **Value structure**: do a few clear masses carry the picture? **Form**: do the bands of light turn the objects round? **Edges**: is there a mix of hard, soft and lost? **Composition**: does the arrangement lead the eye? **Process**: did you go from large to small, and keep to the time budget?

Score each from 1 to 5, as in the figure, and add them: here the total is 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 4 = 20 out of 30. The total matters less than the shape of the scores. The lowest is edges, with 2, so that is the thing to practise next, and one good score on its own proves little.

diagram.alt: A bar for each of six review criteria scored from 1 to 5: proportion 3, value structure 4, form 3, edges 2, composition 4 and process 4. The edges bar is highlighted as the lowest. The total is 20 out of 30.
diagram.caption: An example review. The lowest score, edges, is the criterion to practise next.

reveal.text: Each criterion names one thing to look at. The shape of the scores matters more than the total, because the lowest one tells you what to practise next.
A short, steady habit is the point, in the form of some drawing every day and not a long session now and then.
Composition scored 2 and every other criterion scored 3 or more, so composition is the next target.

lessons.orientation: Put the stages in order, split the time, step back, and review a study against criteria.
lessons.nextAction: Draw a complete study from your own set-up and review it, then repeat the weakest stage.

blocks.text: Give yourself one hour for a still life of a mug and an apple. How would you spend it? Most people start with the part they like, perhaps the handle of the mug, and spend forty minutes on it before they notice that the apple has nowhere to go.

A better plan divides the hour in advance: a few minutes to plan, a few to place the large shapes, the largest share to values, then edges and a last check. The figure shows the hour cut that way, with the minutes for each stage.
