intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the stages of a study in order, split a time budget by percentages, and score a study against six criteria.
intro.whyItMatters: A process turns the skills of the course into a whole study, and a review shows what to practise next.

recap.keyIdea: Work from large to small on a time plan, step back often, and score each study against six criteria.

blocks.text: A study goes from a plan through a block-in, values and edges to a final check, and each stage rests on the one before. A time budget of 10, 20, 40, 20 and 10 percent gives a one-hour study 6, 12, 24, 12 and 6 minutes.

Stepping back makes a drawing look smaller in proportion to the distance, which shows errors that closeness hides, and a six-criterion review with its lowest score tells you what to practise next in short, regular sessions.

questions.prompt: A ruler laid along line A reads 100 units. What will it read along line B?
hints: Ask what was changed between the two lines: the shaft, or only its ends?
The ruler touches the shaft from one end to the other.
If the shafts match, the readings match.
questions.onCorrect: The shafts were drawn at the same length. The fins and arrowheads change how long each line looks, and they do not change the measurement.

misconceptions.feedback: The ends can make a line look shorter, but a ruler reads only the shaft, from one end to the other. Ask whether the two shafts differ.
The ends can make a line look longer, but a ruler reads only the shaft, from one end to the other. Ask whether the two shafts differ.

acceptedIdeas: Exactly 100 units
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exactly 100 units

choices.label: Less than 100 units
More than 100 units
Exactly 100 units

questions.prompt: A student draws a chair and each leg looks right on its own, but the gap between the two front legs looks like a tall doorway. Which fault does the gap point to?
hints: The gap is a shape with a height and a width, and it is judged against the seat.
If the gap is too tall, ask which parts bound it from above and from below.

acceptedIdeas: The legs are drawn too long for the width of the seat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The legs are drawn too long for the width of the seat

questions.onCorrect: The gap has a height and a width like any other shape, so a gap that is too tall tells you the legs are too long, even though you were looking at empty space.

choices.label: The gap is empty space, so it cannot be wrong at all
The legs are drawn too long for the width of the seat
The gap is drawn too dark against the floor behind it
The legs are drawn too thick for the seat they hold

misconceptions.feedback: Empty space has an outline and a size like any shape, and it is the quickest way to find an error because no symbol is stored for it.
The gap is a question of size and shape here. How dark it is does not make a doorway of it.
Thick legs would make the gap narrower, and the trouble here is its height.

questions.prompt: The height is 5 parts and the width is 0.4 of the height. How many parts wide is the door?
hints: The width is 0.4 of the height.
Find 0.4 of 5.
0.4 × 5 is the same as 4 × 5 ÷ 10.
questions.onCorrect: Two parts across against five up is a ratio of 5 to 2, whatever size the door is drawn.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the width as a fraction of the height. Multiply it by the 5 parts we gave the height.
5 parts is the height. The width is shorter, 0.4 of it.

questions.prompt: A student sights a window with a pencil and finds that its width is three quarters of its height. Her drawing of it is a square. What should she change?
hints: Call the height four parts and ask how many parts across the square has, and how many the window has.
Check the drawing against the same comparison you made on the window.

acceptedIdeas: Make the width three quarters of the height
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Make the width three quarters of the height

questions.onCorrect: Three across for every four up is the shape of the window, so a square is too wide at any size. The comparison with the height is what the drawing has to match.

choices.label: Make the drawing wider so it fills the page
Keep the square, since the proportions only matter in the corners
Make the width three quarters of the height
Make the drawing smaller and leave its shape alone

misconceptions.feedback: Width and height have to keep the same ratio as the window, and a square is already too wide for three quarters.
The ratio of width to height holds for the whole shape. A square says the window is as wide as it is tall.
Changing the size alone leaves the ratio as it was, so the drawing is still a square.

questions.prompt: You are about to draw a chair that stands in front of you. Which way of starting keeps its legs, seat and back in proportion with one another?
hints: Ask what each new part is compared with, and whether that thing is already correct.
Think about how a small error early on grows by the end.
questions.onCorrect: A large outline gives every later mark a frame, so a mistake is spotted while it is still big and cheap to correct.

misconceptions.feedback: Legs are easy to recognise, but each part placed after them is judged by eye against the last one, so errors accumulate.
A finished leg gives the rest nothing reliable to be measured against, and an early error is carried into every part that follows.
The seat is only one part. Guessing at the others brings back the habit of drawing what you know.

choices.label: Draw the seat in detail and guess the rest as you go
Draw one leg in careful detail, then add the rest around it
Draw the whole outline and its large spaces first
Draw the legs first, since they are the most recognisable part

acceptedIdeas: Draw the whole outline and its large spaces first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Draw the whole outline and its large spaces first

questions.prompt: Two lines look different in length, one with arrowhead ends and one with outward fins. How can you tell whether their shafts are really equal?
hints: Which of these gives you a measurement and not another impression?
Think about the dashed guides in the figure.
questions.onCorrect: A guide line settles it, because it turns a judgement into a comparison of two ends against one line.

misconceptions.feedback: The effect stays however long you look, because it comes from how the eye judges length in context.
Squinting changes what you see but not the habit of the eye, and the result still depends on impression.
Opinions of viewers only report the impression. The question is about the actual lengths.

choices.label: Look at them for longer until the difference fades
Ask whether most people see them as equal
Compare them against a straight edge at the ends
Squint, so the ends blur and the shafts stand out

acceptedIdeas: Compare them against a straight edge at the ends
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compare them against a straight edge at the ends

questions.prompt: Ruskin wrote this note for people learning to draw. Which habit does it ask of someone about to draw a face?
hints: Ruskin says what the eye receives before experience gives it a meaning.
Ask what a blind man suddenly given sight would see first.

acceptedIdeas: Look at the patches of tone before naming the features
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Look at the patches of tone before naming the features

extracts.text: The whole technical power of painting depends on our recovery of what may be called the innocence of the eye; that is to say, of a sort of childish perception of these flat stains of color, merely as such, without consciousness of what they signify,--as a blind man would see them if suddenly gifted with sight.
extracts.who: John Ruskin, The Elements of Drawing (Project Gutenberg edition)
extracts.kind: A drawing manual written as three letters to beginners

questions.onCorrect: A flat stain of tone is what the eye receives before experience turns it into a face. Drawing starts from the stains and leaves the names until later.

choices.label: Look at the patches of tone before naming the features
Learn the name of every feature first, so that none is missed
Draw each feature as you know it looks, then add the tone
Glance at the face briefly so the detail does not distract you

misconceptions.feedback: Naming is the habit Ruskin wants set aside. A name brings its stored symbol with it.
That is drawing a symbol. Ruskin asks for the flat patches as they appear, before any meaning is attached.
Looking less does not help. The aim is to see the patches themselves, one against another.

questions.prompt: Six things a student did while drawing a chair are listed here. Which came from what she knew about chairs, and which from what she saw?
hints: A symbol is a stored picture, so ask whether the mark could have been made with the chair out of sight.
A gap and a ratio can only be found by looking.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The equal legs, the flat rectangular seat and the complete back came from what she knew. The gap under the seat, the one-and-a-third ratio and the dark patch came from what she saw.

items.label: She drew four straight legs of equal length, though the chair stood at an angle
items.explanation: Equal legs are the stored idea of a chair. At an angle the nearer legs are longer and the farther ones overlap.

items.label: She drew the gap under the seat as its own shape and checked it against the seat
items.explanation: Nobody has a stored symbol for a gap, so drawing it means looking.

items.label: She drew the seat as a flat rectangle, though only a slanted sliver showed
items.explanation: The rectangle is what a seat is in the mind. The sliver is what she saw.

items.label: She found the chair's height to be one and a third of its width and drew it that way
items.explanation: A ratio taken with a pencil comes from the chair itself.

items.label: She drew the back as a neat rectangle, though a leg hid part of it
items.explanation: A hidden part belongs to the idea of the chair and is missing from what can be seen.

items.label: She drew the shape of the dark patch between the back and the seat
items.explanation: The dark patch is a shape in front of her, and it can be compared with the shapes beside it.

questions.onCorrect: Each mark that came from knowledge could have been drawn with the chair out of sight, and each mark that came from sight could not.

questions.prompt: A student ghosts a long line and draws it with her fingers and wrist, and it bows like a shallow bowl. What should she change?
hints: A pen that turns about a point draws part of a circle around that point.
Ask where the pivot should be for a long line, and how that changes the curve.

acceptedIdeas: Swing from the shoulder, so the pivot is far from the pen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swing from the shoulder, so the pivot is far from the pen

questions.onCorrect: A far pivot draws an arc of large radius, which is nearly straight over the length of the line. A pivot at the wrist draws a tight arc, which is why long lines come from the shoulder.

choices.label: Press harder on the paper, so the pen cannot drift off the line
Draw it in several short strokes joined end to end
Move more slowly, so the hand can correct the curve
Swing from the shoulder, so the pivot is far from the pen

misconceptions.feedback: Pressure does not change the path of the pen. The bow comes from the pivot.
Joined strokes bring back the hesitant blur that one stroke avoids, and every join is a small error.
Slowing down invites correction, and the corrections pile up. The arc is set by the pivot.

questions.prompt: An apple rests on a table, lit from the right. Where is a heavier line most useful?
hints: Heavier lines suggest shadow and nearness.
Which side of the apple does the light not reach?

acceptedIdeas: On the left side and at the base on the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: On the left side and at the base on the table

questions.onCorrect: Weight follows light: shadow, contact and overlaps get heavy lines, and the lit edges get thin ones.

choices.label: Along the right side, which faces the light
On the highlight at the top right
On every line, so the outline is easy to read
On the left side and at the base on the table

misconceptions.feedback: Heavier lines suggest shadow and contact, and the side facing the light is where the lines should be lightest.
A highlight is the brightest spot, so it is left as light as possible or left blank.
Equal weight on every line is what makes a drawing look flat. Heavy lines belong where the form is in shadow or in contact.

questions.prompt: A student draws a mug as one even line all the way round its outline, and it looks like a card cut-out. What does the drawing lack?
hints: An outline says where the form ends. Ask what could say how its surface turns.
Think of the cup wrapped in string.

acceptedIdeas: Curved lines across the form, showing how it turns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Curved lines across the form, showing how it turns

questions.onCorrect: Cross-contour lines are slices through the form. They show the roundness that an outline leaves out, and the shape stops reading as a flat patch.

choices.label: A heavier line, so the outline stands out from the page
Curved lines across the form, showing how it turns
A faster outline, drawn in a single quick stroke
A second outline drawn close to the first one

misconceptions.feedback: A heavier line of the same weight all round keeps the outline just as flat.
Speed helps a line stay confident, and it does nothing to describe the surface inside the outline.
A double outline repeats where the form ends and still says nothing about how it turns.

questions.prompt: Why do we ghost the line before drawing it?
hints: Does ghosting leave a mark?
Ask where the hesitation is meant to go.
questions.onCorrect: Ghosting separates planning from marking, so the pen only touches paper once the motion is already smooth.

misconceptions.feedback: Ghosting leaves no mark on the paper. A mark would defeat the point of drawing a single clean line.
Drawing from the wrist is what ghosting from the shoulder is meant to avoid.
A slow line wobbles. The motion is rehearsed so that it can be made at an even, confident speed.

choices.label: So that the line can then be drawn slowly and very carefully
So that the doubt is spent in the air, not on the paper
So that the paper is lightly marked with a guide line
So that the wrist can do the work of the arm

acceptedIdeas: So that the doubt is spent in the air, not on the paper
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: So that the doubt is spent in the air, not on the paper

questions.prompt: You have thirty seconds to draw a seated figure. Which first stroke fits a gesture drawing?
hints: Thirty seconds leaves no time for edges.
Ask which stroke fixes the way the whole figure is arranged.

acceptedIdeas: The curve of the back, in one stroke from the shoulder
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The curve of the back, in one stroke from the shoulder

questions.onCorrect: The curve of the back fixes the arrangement of the whole figure, and the thigh and shin can then follow its direction.

choices.label: The outline of the nearest hand, drawn very carefully
A ruled box around the head, measured to size
The eyes, so that the face is right from the start
The curve of the back, in one stroke from the shoulder

misconceptions.feedback: A hand is a small part. In thirty seconds the largest decision comes first, or the detail has nothing to sit on.
Measuring is slow, and a gesture is made in a few fast strokes before any measuring.
Features are details, and a perfect face on a badly arranged body does not rescue the drawing.

questions.prompt: Six drawing exercises are described here. Which is a contour, which a cross-contour and which a gesture?
hints: A gesture is fast and follows the movement of the whole subject.
A contour follows an edge, and a cross-contour goes across the form.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The runner and the sleeping cat are gestures, the leaf and the bowl's rim are contours, and the lines wrapped round the cup and across the bowl are cross-contours.

items.label: Five strokes in thirty seconds, following the lean of a runner's back, thigh and shin
items.explanation: It records movement and direction fast, with no time for edges.

items.label: A slow line that follows the edge of a leaf as the eye travels along it
items.explanation: The pen follows the edge of the form.

items.label: Curved lines wrapped around a cup, as if it were tied with string
items.explanation: Each line is a slice across the form, showing how the surface turns.

items.label: A few quick curves that catch the sweep of a sleeping cat's body
items.explanation: It fixes the arrangement of the whole subject before any detail.

items.label: The rim, the side and the base of a bowl followed in one unbroken line
items.explanation: The line stays on the boundary of the form.

items.label: Lines across the inside of a bowl that bow the same way to show its depth
items.explanation: They go across the surface and show its curve, as slices would.

questions.onCorrect: A contour travels along an edge, a cross-contour goes across the form, and a gesture records the movement of the whole subject before either.

questions.prompt: A drawing of a ball resting on a table has every line the same weight, and it looks flat. What change would help most?
hints: Think of where the shadow is on the ball.
Which part of the outline is touching something?
questions.onCorrect: Contact and shadow get the weight, which makes the ball sit on the table and turn away from the light.

misconceptions.feedback: A thicker pen keeps every line equal, so the drawing stays flat.
Many short strokes make the hesitant blur the first screen warned against, and do not say where the shadow is.
The lit side should be lightest. The heavy line goes where the form is in shadow or in contact.

choices.label: Redraw the whole outline with a much thicker pen
Add many short strokes to every line of the outline
Make the lit side of the ball the heaviest line of all
Draw the base and the shadow side with heavier lines

acceptedIdeas: Draw the base and the shadow side with heavier lines
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Draw the base and the shadow side with heavier lines

questions.prompt: A student draws a mug with an even line, except for one heavier stroke where the handle joins the body. What is that stroke saying?
hints: Weight is a decision made for each line.
Think about which form is in front where two forms overlap.

acceptedIdeas: That the handle passes in front of the body at the join
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the handle passes in front of the body at the join

questions.onCorrect: A heavier line where one form overlaps another says which is in front, in the same way as heavy lines at the base and in shadow say contact and turning from the light.

choices.label: That the handle is darker in colour than the body of the mug
That the handle is lit more strongly than the body
That the handle passes in front of the body at the join
That the pen was pressed hard by accident

misconceptions.feedback: Line weight says nothing about colour. It says where forms overlap, touch or turn from the light.
Lit edges get the lightest lines, so a heavy stroke says the opposite.
A heavy line can be an accident, but a heavy line at an overlap is a way to show which form is in front.

questions.prompt: You sight the width of a window with your arm straight, so the width is one unit. You then bend your arm a little and count how many of those units fit the window's height. Compared with the true height, is the count too high, too low or right?
hints: Hold a pencil nearer to your face, and look at how much of the wall it covers.
Ask whether a larger unit fits into the height more times or fewer.

acceptedIdeas: Too low, because each unit covers more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Too low, because each unit covers more

questions.onCorrect: A closer pencil covers more of the scene, so each unit stands for a longer stretch and fewer of them fit.

choices.label: Too low, because each unit covers more
Too high, because the pencil looks larger
Right, because the thumb mark stays put

misconceptions.feedback: A closer pencil looks larger, so the mark covers more of the scene than before. Ask whether a larger unit fits into the height more times or fewer.
The thumb mark stays on the pencil, but the part of the scene it covers depends on how far the pencil is from your eye.

questions.prompt: A student enlarges a drawing of a block that is 9 cm wide and 12 cm tall. She makes it 16 cm tall and leaves the width at 9 cm. What does the enlargement look like?
hints: Compare the width with the height in the block and in the enlargement.
The factor that scales the height has to scale the width as well.

acceptedIdeas: Too narrow for its height
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Too narrow for its height

questions.onCorrect: One scale factor has to be applied to every length. Here the height grew by 16 over 12 and the width stayed put, so the block is squeezed from the sides.

choices.label: Too wide for its height
The same shape as the block, only bigger
Too narrow for its height
Turned on its side

misconceptions.feedback: The height grew and the width did not, so the drawing is narrower than the block.
The shape is kept only if the width grows by the same factor as the height.
Nothing has been rotated. One length was scaled and the other was left alone.

questions.prompt: How wide, in cm, is the drawing of the tile?
hints: Multiply 28 by 2/7.
28 ÷ 7 = 4 gives one seventh.
Two sevenths is twice that.
questions.onCorrect: The tile is 4 to 3 and the drawing is 8 to 6, which is 4 to 3, so the shape is kept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height of the drawing. Multiply the width, 28, by 2/7.
That is 28 ÷ 7. The factor has a numerator of 2, so multiply that by 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 28 × 2/7 = 8 cm, so the drawing is 8 by 6 cm, the same 4 to 3 shape as the tile.

questions.prompt: A student copies a house onto a grid by moving from a reference with 2 cm squares to a paper grid with squares 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall. What happens to the house?
hints: A grid works because each square is a copy of the other.
Compare how much each direction was scaled.

acceptedIdeas: It is stretched upward, because height was scaled more than width
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is stretched upward, because height was scaled more than width

questions.onCorrect: The squares must stay squares. A grid of 3 by 4 scales the width by 1.5 and the height by 2, so the house comes out too tall for its width, as the block did when only one side was scaled.

choices.label: It is copied exactly, because the squares are still ruled
It is stretched upward, because height was scaled more than width
It is stretched sideways, because width was scaled more than height
It is correct, since only the lines crossing the squares matter

misconceptions.feedback: The ruling is not the point. Squares that are not squares scale the two directions by different amounts.
The width went from 2 to 3 and the height from 2 to 4, so height was scaled more.
The lines are placed by their squares, and the squares themselves are the wrong shape.

questions.prompt: A student sights a standing model and draws the head 5 cm tall and the whole figure 40 cm tall. How many head units tall is her figure?
hints: A head unit is the height of one head.
Ask how many heads of 5 cm fit into the height of the figure.
Once you have the count, compare it with the canons that teachers use.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so the figure is 8 heads tall, which is one of the two common canons.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two lengths. To count heads, divide the height of the figure by the height of one head.
That subtracts one length from the other. The number of heads is how many times the head fits into the figure.

questions.onCorrect: Eight heads is one of the two common canons, so the proportions of her figure are in the usual range. A figure of 6 heads or 10 heads would look like a child or a giant.

questions.prompt: A student begins a standing figure by drawing a head she likes, 4 cm tall, at the top of the page. At 7.5 heads the feet fall off the bottom. What should she have done?
hints: The head is the unit, so the size of the unit depends on the space the whole figure must fill.
Think about which length is fixed first: the head or the page.

acceptedIdeas: Divided the height of the page by 7.5 to find the head first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Divided the height of the page by 7.5 to find the head first

questions.onCorrect: The unit comes from the space: the height available divided by the number of heads. Every other length of the figure follows from it.

choices.label: Drawn the body smaller than seven heads, so that it fits on the page
Started from the feet and let the head fall where it landed
Divided the height of the page by 7.5 to find the head first
Used a head of 4 cm and a canon of 10 heads instead

misconceptions.feedback: Shrinking the canon breaks the proportions of the figure to suit a head that was chosen without checking.
Where the drawing starts is not the fault. The unit was chosen before the space it had to fit was known.
A taller canon makes the figure taller still. The unit has to come from the space available.

questions.prompt: One figure-drawing book says an adult is 7.5 heads tall and another says 8. A student decides that one of the books must be wrong. What does the lesson say?
hints: A canon is a convention for drawing.
Ask whether real people are all the same height in heads.

acceptedIdeas: Both are conventions, and real people vary around them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both are conventions, and real people vary around them

questions.onCorrect: A canon is a teaching convention, and a source that uses one number is not wrong about the other. Real people differ, so a measurement of the model comes first.

choices.label: The 8 head book is right, since 8 is the whole number
The 7.5 head book is right, since it was written first
Both are conventions, and real people vary around them
Both are wrong, because a head cannot be used as a unit

misconceptions.feedback: A whole number is easier to remember, and it is not more accurate. Real figures vary around either canon.
Order of writing decides nothing. Both are rules of thumb that teachers have chosen.
A head is a good unit because it comes with the subject. The canon only says how many of them to expect.

questions.prompt: Sighting a window, a student finds that its height is one and a third of its width. Her drawing is 12 cm tall and 10 cm wide. What is wrong with it?
hints: Work out how many widths of the drawing fit into its height, and compare with one and a third.
A shape that is too wide for its height has a height of less than one and a third widths.

acceptedIdeas: It is too wide for its height
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is too wide for its height

questions.onCorrect: A window with a height of one and a third widths would be 9 cm wide at a height of 12 cm. At 10 cm the drawing is wider than the window it shows.

choices.label: It is too narrow for its height
It is too tall for the page
It is the right shape, since 12 and 10 are close
It is too wide for its height

misconceptions.feedback: The drawing's height is 1.2 times its width, which is less than the window's 1.33 times, so the drawing is wider than it should be.
How tall the drawing is on the page does not decide its shape. Only the ratio of the two sides does.
The ratio of 12 to 10 is 1.2 against 1.33, and a difference of that size shows when the drawing is laid beside the window.

questions.prompt: A drawer redraws a card 8 cm tall instead of 12 cm, and multiplies its width by the same number she used for its height. What is that number called?
hints: It is found by dividing the new size by the old one.
It has two words, and the second is a word for a number you multiply by.

acceptedIdeas: scale factor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: scale factor

questions.onCorrect: The scale factor is 8 over 12, or two thirds, and it applies to every length. Using it on one side only squashes the shape.

misconceptions.feedback: A ratio compares two lengths of one object. The number that takes one drawing to the other, new over old, has its own name.

questions.prompt: A student wants her drawing of a tin can to show its form as well as its shape. Which drawing does that?
hints: A shape is flat. Ask which drawing has something that curves or slants to show depth.
Look at what happens to the top of the can.

acceptedIdeas: A rectangle with a curved top and base
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A rectangle with a curved top and base

questions.onCorrect: The ellipse and the curve at the base are lines that cross the form, and they are what turns a flat patch into a can with depth.

choices.label: A rectangle with a curved top and base
A circle with a dot at its centre, drawn very neatly
A rectangle filled with an even grey tone
A rectangle drawn in a heavy outline all round

misconceptions.feedback: A circle with a dot is a flat shape, and nothing in it shows the depth of a can.
A grey fill is flat. It gives the shape a tone and no depth.
A heavy outline stresses the edge of a flat shape. A form needs lines that curve across its surface.

questions.prompt: A student sits with her eyes only a little above a table and draws a plate on it as a nearly round ellipse. What is wrong?
hints: The minor axis is the diameter times the sine of the angle between line of sight and the plate.
Ask whether a small angle gives a thin ellipse or a round one.

acceptedIdeas: The ellipse is too open, since a low view gives a thin one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ellipse is too open, since a low view gives a thin one

questions.onCorrect: A small angle gives a small sine, so the minor axis is short and the ellipse is thin. It only becomes round as the line of sight steepens toward straight down.

choices.label: The ends of the ellipse should be more pointed, like a lemon
The ellipse is too open, since a low view gives a thin one
The ellipse is too thin, since a plate is really a circle
The plate should be a straight line at every eye height

misconceptions.feedback: An ellipse is smooth and rounded at both ends. Pointed ends draw a lemon.
A plate is a circle in space, and it only looks like one from straight above.
A straight line is the view exactly at the level of the plate. A little above it, the line opens into a thin ellipse.

questions.prompt: An ellipse has a minor axis of 90 units and a major axis of 120 units. Is the line of sight steeper or shallower than 30° above the plane of the circle?
hints: Find the ratio of the minor axis to the major axis, and compare it with 0.5.
Ask whether this ellipse is thinner or rounder than the one at 30°.

acceptedIdeas: Steeper than 30°
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Steeper than 30°

questions.onCorrect: The ratio 90 ÷ 120 = 0.75 is greater than 0.5, the ratio at 30°, so the ellipse is more open and the line of sight is steeper.

choices.label: Exactly 30°
Shallower than 30°
Steeper than 30°

misconceptions.feedback: At 30° the minor axis is half the major axis, which would be 60 units here.
A shallower view gives a thinner ellipse, with a ratio below one half. Compare 90 ÷ 120 with one half.

questions.prompt: Why can the ratio of the two axes tell us the viewing angle?
hints: Divide the minor axis by the diameter and see what is left.
The ratio of the axes is the minor axis over the major axis.

acceptedIdeas: The minor axis is the diameter times sin α
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The minor axis is the diameter times sin α

questions.onCorrect: Dividing the minor axis by the diameter leaves sin α, so the ratio of the axes is the sine of the viewing angle.

choices.label: The major axis grows as the line of sight steepens
Every ellipse has a minor axis half its major axis
The minor axis is the diameter times sin α
The ratio of the axes is the same at every angle

misconceptions.feedback: The major axis always keeps the full diameter. Only the minor axis changes with the angle.
Different angles give different ratios. A ratio of one half belongs to 30° only.
The ratio changes with the angle, from nearly nothing at eye level to 1 from straight above. That change is what lets it show the angle.

questions.prompt: What is the minor axis, in cm, of a circle 20 cm across seen at 30° to its plane?
hints: Use minor = diameter × sin α.
Half of 20.
questions.onCorrect: Working forward from the angle gives back the measured 10 cm, so the two directions agree.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the major axis, the full diameter.
That uses cos 30° in place of sin 30°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 × sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 cm, which agrees with the ellipse we started from.

questions.prompt: A cylinder lies on its side with its axis horizontal. Is the major axis of the ellipse at its end horizontal or vertical?
hints: The long direction of the ellipse is at right angles to the cylinder's axis.
Where does the cylinder's axis point?

acceptedIdeas: Vertical
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Vertical

questions.onCorrect: The major axis is at right angles to the cylinder's axis, so on a cylinder lying on its side it stands upright, and the minor axis is horizontal.

choices.label: Horizontal
Vertical

misconceptions.feedback: The long direction of the end ellipse is at right angles to the cylinder's axis, and this axis points across your view.

questions.prompt: A student draws a can seen from slightly above, and gives its top and its base the same ellipse. How does the can look?
hints: Ask which end is nearer to eye level.
The ellipse is narrowest at eye level and rounds as it gets farther above or below.

acceptedIdeas: Like a flat stencil, because the base should be rounder than the top
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Like a flat stencil, because the base should be rounder than the top

questions.onCorrect: The base lies farther below eye level, so it is seen at a steeper angle and is rounder. Giving both ends one ellipse makes the can look like a stencil.

choices.label: Right, since both ends are circles of the same size
Like a flat stencil, because the base should be rounder than the top
Like a flat stencil, because the top should be rounder than the base
Right, since the minor axis is vertical for both

misconceptions.feedback: Both ends are the same circle in space, and they are seen at different angles because they are at different heights.
The top is the end nearer eye level, so it is the narrower of the two.
The axis rule does put both minor axes along the can, and it does not make the two ellipses equal in openness.

questions.prompt: The ellipse at the end of each cylinder below has a minor axis. Which way does it run on the page?
hints: The minor axis lies along the axis of the cylinder.
Picture the line from one end of each object to the other.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tin and the flowerpot have vertical minor axes, the log and the barrel horizontal ones, and the tower of cups and the bottle lean, so their minor axes lean with them.

items.label: A tin standing upright on a table
items.explanation: Its axis is vertical, so the minor axis of its ellipses is too.

items.label: A log lying across your view from left to right
items.explanation: Its axis is horizontal, so the minor axes of its ends are horizontal.

items.label: A tower of paper cups leaning at 30°
items.explanation: The axis leans, and the minor axes lean with it.

items.label: A flowerpot standing upright on a shelf
items.explanation: An upright pot has a vertical axis.

items.label: A barrel lying on its side with its ends left and right
items.explanation: The axis runs left to right, so the minor axes do.

items.label: A bottle leaning against a wall
items.explanation: The axis follows the bottle, so the ellipse at its mouth tilts too.

questions.onCorrect: In every case the minor axis follows the object's own axis, which is why it is found by drawing that axis first.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the ellipse at the end of a cylinder is true?
hints: Think of a cylinder lying on its side.
Ask which way the cylinder's own axis points in each view.
questions.onCorrect: The axis rule gives us a way of placing the ellipse for a cylinder pointing in any direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The minor axis follows the cylinder, so on a cylinder that tilts or lies on its side it does too.
An ellipse is smooth and rounded at both ends.
Both the near and the far edges of the circle are curves.

choices.label: Its near edge is flat, while the far edge is curved
Its minor axis is always horizontal on the page
Its minor axis lies along the cylinder's own axis
Its ends are pointed where the long axis meets them

acceptedIdeas: Its minor axis lies along the cylinder's own axis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its minor axis lies along the cylinder's own axis

questions.prompt: A student looks at the rim of an open tin from a little above and sees a thin ellipse. She stands up and looks from higher. What happens to the ellipse?
hints: The ratio of the axes is the sine of the angle between the line of sight and the rim.
Does the angle grow or shrink as her eye rises?

acceptedIdeas: It opens, since the angle and its sine grow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It opens, since the angle and its sine grow

questions.onCorrect: A steeper line of sight gives a larger sine, so the minor axis grows toward the full diameter. Looking straight down at the rim gives a circle.

choices.label: It opens, since the angle and its sine grow
It stays the same, since the rim has not changed
It narrows toward a line
Its major axis shrinks and its minor axis stays

misconceptions.feedback: The rim is the same circle, and the angle from which it is seen has changed. That is what decides the ellipse.

questions.prompt: Three identical trees stand in a row in a drawing. The artist redraws the middle one so that it hides part of each neighbour. What does this tell the viewer, and what does it leave open?
hints: Ask which tree is in front, and then whether the drawing says by how much.
Overlap gives an order.

acceptedIdeas: The middle tree is nearest, but not how far apart the trees are
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The middle tree is nearest, but not how far apart the trees are

questions.onCorrect: Overlap gives the order of the trees and not the gaps between them, so it is usually combined with size and placement.

choices.label: The middle tree is largest, and the others are the same size
The side trees are in shadow, and the middle one is lit
The middle tree is nearest, but not how far apart the trees are
The three trees are the same distance away

misconceptions.feedback: Size is a separate cue. Overlap changes nothing about how large the trees are.
Hiding a part of a neighbour says nothing about light. It is a statement about position.
If they were the same distance away, none of them could hide another.

questions.prompt: Two identical fence posts stand on level ground, and the second is twice as far from the viewer as the first. How tall should the second be drawn?
hints: Drawn height is inversely proportional to distance.
Doubling the distance does something to the height. Ask what.

acceptedIdeas: Half the height of the first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Half the height of the first

questions.onCorrect: Drawn height is inversely proportional to distance, so each doubling of the distance halves it.

choices.label: A quarter of the height of the first
Two thirds of the height of the first
The same height, paler in tone
Half the height of the first

misconceptions.feedback: A quarter is the effect on the area of a flat shape. The height itself halves when the distance doubles.
Heights do not fall by a fixed step. They fall in proportion to the distance, so twice as far is half as tall.
Paleness is haze and it is another cue. The size of the post still falls with distance.

questions.prompt: Eight things are noticed in drawings of landscapes. Which depth cue does each one use?
hints: Ask whether the change is about order, height in the picture, a repeated pattern, or paler and softer tone.
Texture gradient needs a surface with a repeating pattern.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fence post and the boat are overlap, the far walkers and the far sheep are vertical placement, the cobbles and the corn are texture gradient, and the pale hills and the smoky valley are atmospheric perspective.

items.label: A fence post hides part of the barn behind it
items.explanation: One thing covers part of another, so it is read as nearer.

items.label: The farthest range of hills is pale and has lost its detail
items.explanation: Air between viewer and hills lightens and softens each layer.

items.label: Cobblestones shrink and close up along the street
items.explanation: A repeating pattern changes at a steady rate with distance.

items.label: The soles of the far walkers sit higher on the page than those of the near ones
items.explanation: On level ground the bases of farther things lie nearer the horizon.

items.label: A boat in front of the headland cuts across its lower part
items.explanation: The boat hides a piece of the headland, which places it in front.

items.label: Each row of corn is finer and closer to the next than the row before
items.explanation: The rows are a repeating pattern that tightens toward the horizon.

items.label: A smoky valley has lost contrast between the trees and the sky
items.explanation: Loss of contrast with distance is the mark of atmospheric perspective.

items.label: The farthest sheep stand higher in the field than the nearest
items.explanation: Their bases are placed nearer the horizon on the page.

questions.onCorrect: Each cue has its own sign: one thing covering another, a base higher on the page, a pattern that tightens, and tone that softens with distance.

questions.prompt: How tall, in cm, is the figure drawn at 25 m?
hints: Height equals the constant divided by the distance.
The constant is 40, so divide 40 by the new distance.

questions.onCorrect: At 25 m the figure is drawn 1.6 cm, between the 2 cm of 20 m and the 1 cm of 40 m, as it should be.

questions.prompt: A flat sign is moved to four times its distance, so its drawn height and width are each a quarter of what they were. How much of its first drawn area does it cover?
hints: Area is height times width.

acceptedIdeas: A sixteenth, since both lengths shrink to a quarter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A sixteenth, since both lengths shrink to a quarter

questions.onCorrect: Area follows the square of the scale factor, so a quarter of each length leaves a sixteenth of the area.

choices.label: A quarter, since the rule is a quarter of each length
A half, since half the lengths remain visible
An eighth, since three of the four sides move
A sixteenth, since both lengths shrink to a quarter

misconceptions.feedback: A quarter is the factor for each length. The area is the product of two lengths, so both factors apply.

questions.prompt: A drawing of a city skyline shows the nearest tower dark and sharp, and each tower behind it lighter and softer, with fewer windows. Which depth cue does this use?
hints: The change in tone comes from the air in between.

questions.onCorrect: Haze lightens and softens distant layers, so an artist can show depth with tone alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Overlap says which object is in front, and does not change tone.

choices.label: Overlap of the towers
Vertical placement

Atmospheric perspective

questions.prompt: A student draws a forest at night, and decides to make the farthest trees paler and bluer, as in a daytime landscape. What is wrong?
hints: The rule is loss of contrast, which does not always mean lighter.

acceptedIdeas: The farthest trees should melt into the dark with less detail
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The farthest trees should melt into the dark with less detail

questions.onCorrect: The rule is loss of contrast with distance. In a dark scene the air is dark, so the distant trees blend into it and show less detail rather than turning pale.

choices.label: The farthest trees should be sharper than the nearest
Distance has no effect on trees at night
The farthest trees should be larger, since the dark hides size
The farthest trees should melt into the dark with less detail

misconceptions.feedback: Distance softens detail in any light. The farthest trees lose edges and contrast.
Air between the viewer and the trees still blurs them. At night the air is dark.

questions.prompt: Leonardo listed three branches of perspective. In a drawing of a row of hills, which change belongs to the third branch?
hints: Match each change to the branch: smaller, a different colour, or less finished.

acceptedIdeas: Leaving out windows and fine detail on the farthest hills
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaving out windows and fine detail on the farthest hills

extracts.text: There are three branches of perspective; the first deals with the reasons of the (apparent) diminution of objects as they recede from the eye, and is known as Diminishing Perspective.--The second contains the way in which colours vary as they recede from the eye. The third and last is concerned with the explanation of how the objects [in a picture] ought to be less finished in proportion as they are remote
extracts.who: Leonardo da Vinci, Notebooks (translated by Jean Paul Richter)
extracts.when: an entry that Richter dates before 1490 from the handwriting
extracts.kind: A private working note for a planned book on painting

questions.onCorrect: The third branch asks for less finish on what is far away. Size belongs to the first branch and colour to the second.

choices.label: Drawing the farthest hills smaller than the nearest ones in the row
Leaving out windows and fine detail on the farthest hills
Drawing the farthest hills paler and bluer
Setting the farthest hills higher on the page

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first branch, the diminishing of objects as they recede.
That is the second branch, the way colours vary as they recede.
Placement belongs with the first branch, which deals with the apparent diminishing of objects.

questions.prompt: A row of identical posts runs away from you across level ground. The farther posts have their bases higher up the picture than the nearer ones. Which cue is this?
hints: The cue is about where the bases are placed.

questions.onCorrect: On level ground, the base of a farther object sits nearer the horizon, so it is placed higher in the picture.

misconceptions.feedback: Overlap needs one object to cover part of another, which is not described here.
Atmospheric perspective is about paleness and lost contrast.

choices.label: Overlap
Vertical placement
Texture gradient
Atmospheric perspective

acceptedIdeas: Vertical placement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Vertical placement

questions.prompt: A drawing of a cobbled street makes the stones near the viewer large and widely spaced, and the stones near the end of the street small and closely packed. Which depth cue is this?
hints: Think about the pattern itself, and about how it changes with distance.

questions.onCorrect: A texture gradient needs a surface with a repeating pattern, and it shows how fast that surface recedes.

acceptedIdeas: texture gradient
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: texture gradient

questions.prompt: You stand in a field with your eyes 1.6 m above the ground, and you look at a tree 20 m away. The horizon is the line at the level of your own eyes. Where does the horizon line cross the trunk of that tree?
hints: The horizon is a line at your own eye level.
How high is your eye?
It does not change with the tree's distance.
questions.onCorrect: The horizon is the viewer's eye level, so it crosses everything at the same height above level ground, however far away it is.

misconceptions.feedback: The horizon is not where the ground ends. Look again at how the question defines it.

acceptedIdeas: 1.6 m up the trunk, level with your eyes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1.6 m up the trunk, level with your eyes

choices.label: At the base, where the trunk meets the ground
Higher up the trunk the farther away the tree is
1.6 m up the trunk, level with your eyes

questions.prompt: A student draws a straight road with its edges meeting at a point halfway up the sky, well above the horizon line she drew at eye level. What is wrong?
hints: The lines meet where the road goes out of sight, level with the viewer's eyes.
Ask which line in the drawing marks eye level.

acceptedIdeas: The road edges should meet on the horizon line, level with her eyes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The road edges should meet on the horizon line, level with her eyes

questions.onCorrect: The edges of a level road recede to a point on the horizon, because the vanishing point of level lines is at eye level.

choices.label: The road edges should be parallel in the drawing, since they are parallel in life
The road edges should meet at the bottom of the picture
The road edges should meet on the horizon line, level with her eyes
The road edges should meet wherever the sky begins

misconceptions.feedback: Parallel lines that recede are drawn converging. A drawing of parallel edges would show a road that never gets narrower.

questions.prompt: Why is the back face scaled by the ratio of the two distances?
hints: Recall the size rule from the last lesson.
Equal lengths at different distances are drawn at different sizes.

acceptedIdeas: Drawn size falls in proportion as distance grows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Drawn size falls in proportion as distance grows

questions.onCorrect: Drawn height is inversely proportional to distance, so a face at 5 m is drawn 4 ÷ 5 as large as the same face at 4 m.

Drawn size falls in proportion as distance grows
The vanishing point is 4 m from the front face
Every box is drawn at a fixed scale of 0.8

misconceptions.feedback: A real box has equal faces at the front and the back. Only their distances from you differ.
The vanishing point lies on the horizon in the picture. It is not a distance from the box.

questions.prompt: The back face is scaled by 0.8 from a front face 90 units tall. How tall, in units, is the back face?
hints: Use the factor 0.8.
A factor of 0.8 is four fifths.
Four fifths of 90: divide 90 by 5, then multiply by 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the front face. The back face is farther away, so it is smaller.

questions.prompt: A student draws a long box in one-point perspective with its back face the same size as its front face. What does the box look like?
hints: The back face is farther from the viewer than the front face.

acceptedIdeas: Too big, the back face should be smaller than the front
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Too big, the back face should be smaller than the front

choices.label: Right, since both faces are squares of the same size
Too small, since it should be bigger at the back than the front
Too big, the back face should be smaller than the front

questions.prompt: A box in a drawing shows its underside and its left side. Where is the box?
hints: Seeing the underside means looking up at the box. Which side face a box shows depends on which side of the vanishing point it is.

acceptedIdeas: Above the horizon and right of the vanishing point

questions.onCorrect: Seeing the underside puts the box above the horizon, and seeing its left side puts it to the right of the vanishing point.

choices.label: Below the horizon and right of the vanishing point
Above the horizon and left of the vanishing point
Above the horizon and right of the vanishing point
Below the horizon and left of the vanishing point

misconceptions.feedback: A box below the horizon is seen from above, so its top shows and its underside does not.
A box to the left of the vanishing point shows its right side. Check which side face this box shows.

questions.prompt: A box sits below the horizon, centred on the line that runs straight down from the vanishing point. Which faces of the box can you see?
hints: Is the box above or below the horizon, and is it to the left or the right of the vanishing point?

acceptedIdeas: Its front and its top
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its front and its top

choices.label: Its front and its underside

Its front, its top and its right side
Its front and its top

misconceptions.feedback: A box below the horizon is seen from above, so its top shows and its underside does not.

questions.prompt: A student builds a box in one-point perspective. In what order should she take these steps?
hints: The horizon decides where everything else goes, so it comes before any box.
The back face needs the orthogonals to shrink toward, so they come first.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She draws the horizon and the vanishing point first, then the square front face, then the orthogonals from its corners, then the smaller back face between them, and last keeps the visible edges.

items: Draw the horizon at eye level and mark the vanishing point on it
Draw the front face as a square
Draw orthogonals from the front corners to the vanishing point
Draw the back face between the orthogonals, smaller than the front
Keep only the edges that can be seen

questions.onCorrect: The horizon comes first because it decides what every box shows. The back face is the last shape drawn, because it can only be placed between orthogonals that already exist.

questions.prompt: Leonardo describes drawing on a pane of glass. Which practice follows from what he writes?
hints: The lines run from each point of the scene to a single point, the eye.

acceptedIdeas: Keep one eye in one place and trace what you see on the glass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep one eye in one place and trace what you see on the glass

These can be traced in pyramids to the point in the eye, and these pyramids are intersected on the glass plane.
extracts.who: Leonardo da Vinci, Notebooks (translated by Jean Paul Richter)
extracts.when: written in his notebooks over many years
extracts.kind: A private working note for a planned book on painting

questions.onCorrect: A drawing in perspective is what one eye sees through a flat surface, so the eye stays fixed. That fixed eye is also why the horizon is at the level of the eye.

choices.label: Move around the glass while tracing, to catch every side
Trace the objects from memory, then check them against the glass
Draw the objects at their real size on the glass
Keep one eye in one place and trace what you see on the glass

misconceptions.feedback: The pyramids end in one point in the eye. Moving changes the point, and the tracing no longer agrees with itself.
The glass is for tracing what is seen through it. A memory brings back the stored symbols.

questions.prompt: A student draws a street from the pavement. She then stands on a chair and draws the same street. What happens to the horizon line in the second drawing?

acceptedIdeas: It moves up the page, since her eye level has risen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It moves up the page, since her eye level has risen

questions.onCorrect: The horizon marks eye level, so a higher eye puts it higher in the picture and shows more of the ground below it.

choices.label: It stays at the same height on the page as before
It moves down the page, since she is higher up
It moves up the page, since her eye level has risen
It disappears, since the street is farther away

misconceptions.feedback: The horizon is set by eye level. A higher eye puts it higher in the picture.
A higher eye puts the horizon higher up, and the ground fills more of the picture.
The horizon does not depend on how far away anything is. It is always there at eye level.

questions.prompt: A cube is turned so that no face is parallel to the picture, and viewed from a level eye height. How many vanishing points do its edges use?

choices.label: One

Both points belong on the same horizon, level with the eye

questions.prompt: Why do the lines from the top of the first vertical edge go to both vanishing points?

Because the vertical edge has two vanishing points
Because the corner has one edge in each direction
Because the horizon has been drawn twice

questions.prompt: A student draws a model with one arm resting across her body and the other pointing straight at the viewer. She draws both arms the same length. What is wrong?

questions.prompt: Ruskin wrote this about the rules of perspective. In your own drawing of a box and a forearm, how would you apply it?

questions.prompt: A student builds a cube in two-point perspective. In what order should she take these steps?
