hints: Count the directions of parallel edges that are not parallel to the picture.
Looking steeply up or down brings in the vertical edges as a direction.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The railway track and the bookshelf need one point, the corner of the house and the turned cube need two, and the tower looked up at and the building looked down on need three.

items.label: Looking straight down a railway track from the sleepers
items.explanation: Only the track runs away from the viewer, so one set of edges recedes.

items.label: A house seen at the corner from the street, with no wall facing you
items.explanation: Two directions of horizontal edge recede, and the verticals stay vertical.

items.label: A tower seen from the pavement with your head tipped back
items.explanation: The horizontal edges recede and the vertical edges converge too.

items.label: A bookshelf seen square-on from across the room
items.explanation: Its front is parallel to the picture, so only the depth edges recede.

items.label: A cube turned so that you look at its corner at eye level
items.explanation: No face is parallel to the picture, so two directions recede.

items.label: A tall building seen from a helicopter looking steeply down
items.explanation: A steep downward view makes the vertical edges converge as well.

questions.onCorrect: The number of points is the number of directions of receding parallel edges, and a steep view tips the vertical edges into receding.

questions.prompt: A house is drawn with its front wall parallel to the picture, from a level eye height. How many vanishing points does its drawing need?
hints: Which edges recede in this view?
How many directions do the receding edges have?
Each direction of receding edges has a point of its own.
questions.onCorrect: One face parallel to the picture means a single set of receding edges, and so a single vanishing point.

misconceptions.feedback: The edges that run away from the viewer still meet at a point on the horizon.
Two are needed only when no face is parallel to the picture.

acceptedIdeas: One
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One

choices.label: None
Two
One

questions.prompt: On a nine-step scale from 100 percent at step 1 to 0 percent at step 9, what is the value, in percent, of step 3?
hints: Nine steps have eight gaps between them.
Each gap is 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5.
Step 3 is two gaps below step 1.
questions.onCorrect: Nine steps make eight equal gaps, so each step is 12.5 points darker than the one before.

misconceptions.feedback: That is step 2. Step 3 is one more gap below it.
That divides 100 into three. The gap is 100 ÷ 8, since nine steps make eight gaps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The gap is 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 points, and step 3 is two gaps from white: 100 − 25 = 75 percent.

questions.prompt: A greyscale copy of a painting shows a red apple on a green cloth as one flat grey, with no edge between them. What do the apple and the cloth share?
hints: What is left when the hues are removed?
Ask what a greyscale copy keeps and what it throws away.

acceptedIdeas: The same value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same value

questions.onCorrect: Where two areas share a value, a greyscale copy shows no edge between them, because value carries the structure of a picture.

choices.label: The same hue
The same value
The same number of colours

misconceptions.feedback: A red apple and a green cloth have different hues, and a greyscale copy removes hue altogether.
A greyscale copy discards colour, so a count of colours cannot be what hides the edge.

questions.prompt: A student draws a white shirt hanging in deep shade as pure white, and a black coat in full sun as pure black. Her drawing looks flat. What went wrong?
hints: Think about what the shirt and the coat look like in those places, and not what colour they are.
Judge each patch by the value you see, comparing it with the ones beside it.

acceptedIdeas: She copied local values from memory and not the values she saw
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She copied local values from memory and not the values she saw

questions.onCorrect: A white shirt in shadow is mid-grey and a black coat in sun is dim. Drawing the local values from memory ignores the light, and the picture goes flat.

choices.label: She used too many values for the number of objects
Local value decides how an object is drawn, so she was right to do it
She copied local values from memory and not the values she saw
A shirt must always be drawn darker than a coat

misconceptions.feedback: The trouble is which values she chose. The count is not the cause.
Local value is a reason for the pattern of values. The light then changes each patch, and the drawing has to show what is seen.
There is no fixed order. A shirt in shade is mid-grey, and a coat in sun may be dim, and the order depends on the light.

questions.prompt: Of pure red, pure green and pure blue at full intensity, which appears lightest when converted to grey?
hints: The eye is not equally sensitive to every colour of light.
Think of how bright each pure colour looks on a screen beside the other two.
questions.onCorrect: The eye is most sensitive to green light, so green carries the largest weight in a grey conversion.

misconceptions.feedback: Red is brighter than blue in grey, but not the brightest of the three.
The three are weighted differently, because the eye is not equally sensitive to them.
Blue is the darkest of the three in grey.

choices.label: Red
Green
All the same
Blue

acceptedIdeas: Green
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Green

questions.prompt: What is the grey level of (200, 100, 50), to the nearest whole number?
hints: Add the three contributions shown in the steps.
The red and green contributions together come to a little over 114.
The blue contribution is 3.61. Add it, then round to the nearest whole number.
questions.onCorrect: A grey level of 118 out of 255 is a mid-dark value, which is about 46 percent light.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the green value alone. Add all three contributions.
That is the grey of pure red. Add the three contributions given.

questions.prompt: What is the grey level, to the nearest whole number, of pure yellow (R 255, G 255, B 0)?
hints: Add the contributions of red and green.
questions.onCorrect: Yellow is almost as light as white in grey, since red and green carry most of the weight, which is why a yellow near white paper is hard to see in a photocopy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is white. Yellow has no blue, and blue carries 0.0722 of the weight.
That is only the green contribution. Red adds 54.

questions.prompt: A student paints a red apple on a green cloth, and in a greyscale copy the apple melts into the cloth. She wants it to stand out in a pencil drawing of the same scene. What should she do?
hints: Pencil has value and no hue.
Ask which attribute separated the apple from the cloth in colour, and which one survives in grey.

acceptedIdeas: Make the apple lighter or darker than the cloth in value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Make the apple lighter or darker than the cloth in value

questions.onCorrect: Where two areas share a value, the edge between them is lost. Giving the apple a different value from the cloth is what restores it.

choices.label: Make the apple a more vivid and saturated red
Outline the apple heavily and keep it the same grey as the cloth
Add more bright colours around the apple
Make the apple lighter or darker than the cloth in value

misconceptions.feedback: Vividness is chroma, and pencil has none. A vivid red and a green of the same lightness are still the same grey.
A heavy outline puts back an edge by force. The values still agree, and the picture still has no edge in its tones.
More colours add hue, and hue is lost in pencil. The structure of the picture rests on value.

questions.prompt: A student's drawing of a pear has fourteen greys that look much alike. What does Speed's advice tell her to do?
hints: Ask how many masses Speed says most objects reduce to.
The small differences are added on top, once the large ones are set.

acceptedIdeas: Gather them into lights, half tones and shadows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Gather them into lights, half tones and shadows

extracts.text: Most objects can be reduced broadly into three tone masses, the lights (including the high lights), the half tones, and the shadows. And the habit of reducing things into a simple equation of three tones as a foundation on which to build complex appearances should early be sought for.
extracts.who: Harold Speed, The Practice and Science of Drawing (Project Gutenberg edition)
extracts.kind: A drawing manual for art students

questions.onCorrect: Three masses give the picture a structure the eye can read, and the finer greys then sit inside them.

choices.label: Gather them into lights, half tones and shadows
Add a fifteenth grey so that no two greys are alike
Keep all fourteen, since each belongs to the pear
Draw only the outline and leave the greys out

misconceptions.feedback: More greys add to the blur. Speed asks for fewer masses, with the complex appearance built on them.
Each may belong to the pear, and a reading of the form needs a few clear masses. Fourteen similar ones blur into one.
Speed does not drop the tones. He reduces them to a simple equation of three, and complex appearances grow from there.

questions.prompt: A white cube and a black cube stand under one lamp, and the shaded side of the white cube is as dark as the lit top of the black one. What name does the lesson give to the lightness each cube has under even light?
hints: It belongs to the object and not to the light.
It has the word local in it.
questions.onCorrect: Local value is what the surface is, and lighting is what happens to it. The values you see combine the two.

acceptedIdeas: local value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: local value

questions.prompt: A student squints at her still life and sees the pear and the plate melt into one patch. What should she change?
hints: Squinting shows the values and hides the detail.
Two similar values blur into one.

acceptedIdeas: Give them clearly different values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Give them clearly different values

questions.onCorrect: The eye reads shape from boundaries between values. Two similar values blur into one shape, and a clear difference separates them.

choices.label: Add a heavy outline to each, and leave the values
Give the pear more detail inside its shape
Give them clearly different values
Make both darker, so that they match the shadow

misconceptions.feedback: Outlines add edges by force while the values still agree. The merge shows that the values need to differ.
Detail sits inside a mass. It does not separate one mass from the one beside it.
Making both darker keeps them alike. The pear and the plate need to differ from each other.

questions.prompt: A lamp shines on a sphere resting on a table, from the upper left as you look at it. Where does the sphere's cast shadow fall?
hints: Light travels in straight lines and the object blocks it.
A shadow lies on the side of the object away from the lamp.
questions.onCorrect: A shadow lies on the line from the light through the object, beyond the object, so it falls away from the light.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the side the light comes from, and the shadow is formed on the opposite side.
A light that is off to one side puts the shadow off to the opposite side, not just under the sphere.
Shadows fall along the line away from the light, not sideways across it.

choices.label: Upper right
Directly beneath it only
Upper left
Lower right

acceptedIdeas: Lower right
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lower right

questions.prompt: A student draws a sphere lit from the upper left, with the reflected light at the shadow edge as bright as the lit side. What does that do to the form?
hints: Reflected light is borrowed from the table and walls.
Ask whether the shadow side should compete with the lit side.

acceptedIdeas: It looks flat, since the shadow side competes with the light
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It looks flat, since the shadow side competes with the light

questions.onCorrect: Reflected light lifts the shadow edge a little and never to the value of the lit side. If it matches, the darkest band disappears and the form flattens.

choices.label: It makes the sphere look glossy, like a billiard ball
It looks flat, since the shadow side competes with the light
It makes the sphere look larger than the lit side suggests it is
Nothing, since reflected light can be any value

misconceptions.feedback: Glossiness is shown by a small sharp highlight. A bright strip at the shadow edge does not suggest it.
Brightness at the edge does not change the apparent size. It changes how the form turns.
Reflected light is never as bright as the lit side, and a drawing that makes it so loses the turn into shadow.

questions.prompt: A student draws a bottle whose cast shadow has the same value from end to end, and the bottle seems to float above the table. What change makes it sit?
hints: The shadow is darkest where the object blocks the most light.
Ask where the bottle touches the table.

acceptedIdeas: Make the shadow darkest at the bottle and lighter with distance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Make the shadow darkest at the bottle and lighter with distance

questions.onCorrect: A contact shadow that is darkest at the bottle and lightens with distance says where the bottle meets the table, and the bottle stops floating.

choices.label: Make the shadow lighter where it meets the base of the bottle
Make the shadow darkest at the bottle and lighter with distance
Make the shadow the same value as the bottle itself and no lighter
Outline the shadow so that its shape is clear to see

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wrong end. The shadow is darkest at the object, where it blocks almost all the light.
Matching the bottle keeps the shadow a flat patch. A shadow lightens as it goes away from the object.
An outline makes the shape clear and does not tell where the bottle touches the table.

questions.prompt: A post 5 m tall casts a shadow 12 m long on level ground. Is the sun higher or lower than 45° above the horizon?
hints: At 45° the shadow is exactly as long as the object is tall.
A longer shadow means a lower sun.

acceptedIdeas: Lower than 45°, since the shadow is longer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lower than 45°, since the shadow is longer

questions.onCorrect: A shadow longer than the object always means a sun lower than 45°, near sunrise or sunset, and not a brighter one.

choices.label: Exactly 45°, since the post is tall and thin
Higher than 45°, since the shadow is so long
Lower than 45°, since the shadow is longer

misconceptions.feedback: At 45° the shadow would be 5 m, the same as the post. This one is longer.
A high sun makes short shadows. A long one means a low sun.

questions.prompt: What is the shadow length, in m, of a child 1.5 m tall with the sun at 30°, to two decimal places?
hints: Divide the height by the tangent.
tan 30° is about 0.5774.
The sun is low, so the shadow is longer than the child is tall.
questions.onCorrect: At 30° a shadow is a little over 1.7 times the height, so 1.5 m becomes about 2.6 m.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 1.5 × tan 30°. Divide by the tangent.
That is the child's height. At 30° the shadow is longer than the child.

questions.prompt: Leonardo wrote this about shadow. What does it suggest for a drawing of a sphere?
hints: Ask what shows the roundness of a sphere that an outline cannot.
Shadow comes in infinite degrees between light and dark.

acceptedIdeas: Its roundness comes from graded shadow, so an outline alone cannot show it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its roundness comes from graded shadow, so an outline alone cannot show it

extracts.text: The beginnings and ends of shadow lie between the light and darkness and may be infinitely diminished and infinitely increased. Shadow is the means by which bodies display their form. The forms of bodies could not be understood in detail but for shadow.
extracts.who: Leonardo da Vinci, Notebooks (translated by Jean Paul Richter)
extracts.when: written in his notebooks over many years
extracts.kind: A private working note for a planned book on painting

questions.onCorrect: A sphere drawn as a bare circle is a flat disc. The graded bands of shadow are what make it a ball, which is why the lesson draws them in order.

choices.label: Its roundness comes from graded shadow, so an outline alone cannot show it
Its roundness comes from a clean line between light and dark
Its shadow is best drawn as one flat dark patch
Its roundness is clear from the outline, and shadow is only decoration

misconceptions.feedback: Leonardo stresses the degrees of shadow between light and darkness. A line with no grading would drop them.
One flat patch has no degrees. Leonardo says shadow may be increased and diminished without limit.
He says forms could not be understood in detail but for shadow. Shadow is what shows them.

questions.prompt: In a drawing of a sunny field, one fence post has a shadow twice as long as the shadow of an identical post beside it. What is wrong?
hints: The sun's rays are close to parallel.
Ask what decides the length of a shadow on level ground.

acceptedIdeas: Identical posts in parallel sunlight cast shadows of equal length
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Identical posts in parallel sunlight cast shadows of equal length

questions.onCorrect: The sun's rays are parallel, so identical vertical posts on level ground have shadows of the same length at the same angle.

choices.label: Nothing, since shadows change with the distance from the viewer's eye
The longer shadow means a brighter lamp placed near that post
The shorter post must be nearer to the sun
Identical posts in parallel sunlight cast shadows of equal length

misconceptions.feedback: Distance from the viewer affects how big the posts look. The length of the shadows is fixed by the sun.
A field in sunlight has one light, and a bright source does not stretch a shadow.
The sun is too far away to matter. Its rays are parallel at both posts.

questions.prompt: A sphere is lit from the upper left. Going across it from the lit side to the shadow edge, in what order do the parts of the light appear?
hints: The highlight is where the surface faces the light most directly.
The terminator is where light turns to shadow, and the darkest band lies just inside it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: From the lit side the order is the highlight, the light, the halftone, the terminator, the core shadow and the reflected light at the very edge.

items: Highlight
Light
Halftone
Terminator
Core shadow
Reflected light

questions.onCorrect: The darkest band is the core shadow, just inside the terminator, and reflected light lifts the edge beyond it.

questions.prompt: Where is the darkest band on a lit sphere?
hints: Which band receives reflected light?
The terminator is the line where the light turns into shadow.
questions.onCorrect: The core shadow is the darkest band, since it receives neither direct light nor much reflected light.

misconceptions.feedback: Reflected light lifts the outer edge, so the edge is lighter than the band inside it.
The highlight is the brightest part, where the surface faces the light.
The halftone lies between the light and the terminator, so it is lit.

choices.label: Just inside the terminator
At the highlight
In the halftone
At its outer edge on the shadow side

acceptedIdeas: Just inside the terminator
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Just inside the terminator

questions.prompt: In a drawing, a post's shadow is half as long as the post is tall. What does that tell the viewer about the sun?
hints: At 45° the shadow equals the height.
A shorter shadow means a higher sun.

acceptedIdeas: It is higher than 45°, so the shadows are short
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is higher than 45°, so the shadows are short

questions.onCorrect: A shadow shorter than the post means a sun higher than 45°, and the shorter it is, the higher the sun.

choices.label: It is higher than 45°, so the shadows are short
It is lower than 45°, so the shadows are short ones
It is exactly 45°, since the shadow is half the post

misconceptions.feedback: A low sun makes long shadows. A shadow that is shorter than the post points to a sun above 45°.
At 45° the shadow is as long as the post. Half the height is shorter than that.

questions.prompt: A dark jacket with a value of 10 percent is seen against a bright window with a value of 90 percent. What kind of edge is the jacket's outline?
hints: Compare the values on the two sides of the boundary.
Ask whether the two values are close together or far apart.

acceptedIdeas: A hard edge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A hard edge

questions.onCorrect: Where the two values are far apart, the change is sudden and the edge is hard.

choices.label: A hard edge
A soft edge
A lost edge
A contour

misconceptions.feedback: A soft edge is a gradual change in value. Here the value jumps from 10 to 90 at the boundary.
A lost edge needs the two values to match, and these are far apart.
A contour is a line that follows an edge, which is not the same as the edge's value change.

questions.prompt: Two patches are hatched with lines of the same width. In one the lines are close together, and in the other they are wide apart. Which looks darker from a reading distance, and why?
hints: From a distance the eye cannot separate the lines.
Ask how much of the paper each patch covers.

acceptedIdeas: The close patch, since its lines cover more of the paper
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The close patch, since its lines cover more of the paper

questions.onCorrect: The close patch has less bare paper between its lines. Coverage is the width of the line divided by the spacing, so closer lines cover more.

choices.label: The wide patch, since each line is easier to see there
They match, since only the width of the line matters
The close patch, since its lines cover more of the paper
Neither, since the eye separates every line from the next

misconceptions.feedback: Visible lines are not darker. From a distance the eye merges the lines into a tone, and the tone depends on coverage.
The width is the same, and the spacing differs, and coverage is the width divided by the spacing.
At a normal reading distance the eye cannot separate the lines, and it merges them into a tone.

questions.prompt: A student wants a hatched patch to look darker without changing her pencil. Which change does the lesson prefer?
hints: The line width stays the same when she changes the spacing.
Think about which change gives tone in predictable steps.

acceptedIdeas: Draw the lines closer together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Draw the lines closer together

questions.onCorrect: Closer spacing keeps the line width and changes the coverage in predictable steps, which is the cleaner way to darken.

choices.label: Press harder on every line she draws
Rub the lines with a finger to smear them
Draw the lines closer together
Draw the lines longer across the patch

misconceptions.feedback: Pressing hard shines the paper, and the tone is hard to adjust afterwards.
Rubbing smooths the tone and removes its texture and its edges.
Length changes how far the patch reaches. The tone depends on how much of the paper the lines cover.

questions.prompt: Two independent layers of hatching each cover 25 percent of the paper. What percentage is covered by the two together?
hints: Work out the share left bare by one layer.
Multiply the bare shares of the two layers.
Subtract the result from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Two 25 percent layers give 43.75 percent, less than the 50 percent that adding would suggest.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two layers, which double counts the places where the lines cross.
That is the bare share. The covered share is the rest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The bare share is 0.75 × 0.75 = 0.5625, so the covered share is 1 − 0.5625 = 0.4375, or 43.75 percent.

questions.prompt: The two layers leave 0.81 of the paper bare. What percentage is covered?
hints: Subtract the bare share from 1.
One minus the bare share is the covered share, as a decimal.
Write it as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Crossing two 10 percent layers gives 19 percent, one point less than the 20 percent that adding would give.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bare share. The covered share is the rest.
That adds the two layers, 10 + 10. The overlap means the true coverage is a little less.

questions.prompt: Which of these pencils is the softest and leaves the darkest mark?
hints: Which letter means soft, and which number means the softest?
B pencils are the soft ones and H pencils the hard ones.

acceptedIdeas: 5B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 5B

questions.onCorrect: A larger number before B means a softer lead and a darker mark, so 5B is the darkest of these.

choices.label: HB
5B
3B
4H

misconceptions.feedback: HB is in the middle of the scale, between the hard and the soft.
3B is soft, but the number says how soft, and one of the other pencils has a larger number.
H pencils are the hard, light ones, and 4H is harder than H.

questions.prompt: A student draws the shadow of an apple lit by a large window with a razor-sharp outline. According to Leonardo, what is wrong?
hints: Ask how large the light source is.
Large lights give less defined outlines.

acceptedIdeas: A large window gives a shadow with a soft, less defined edge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A large window gives a shadow with a soft, less defined edge

extracts.text: That a shadow will have less defined outlines in proportion as the light which causes it is larger, and conversely, the outlines are clearer in proportion as it is smaller.
extracts.who: Leonardo da Vinci, Notebooks (translated by Jean Paul Richter)
extracts.when: written in his notebooks over many years
extracts.kind: A private working note on light and shadow

questions.onCorrect: A large light source gives a soft edge, and a small one a crisp edge. Choosing the edge from the light is part of choosing it from the values on each side.

choices.label: A large window gives a shadow with a soft, less defined edge
A large window gives a sharper shadow than a small lamp does
Shadow edges depend on the apple and not on the light
The shadow should have no edge at all

misconceptions.feedback: Leonardo says the opposite: the outline is clearer as the light is smaller.
Leonardo ties the outline of the shadow to the size of the light that causes it.
He says the outline becomes less defined as the light grows, and an outline still remains.

questions.prompt: Source A is Ruskin writing to beginners, and Source B is Speed describing a painting by Corot. What practice do the two sources support together?
hints: Ask what Source A says an edge really is, and what Source B praises about edges.
Both talk about masses meeting one another.

acceptedIdeas: Edges are where masses meet, sharp in places and lost in others
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Edges are where masses meet, sharp in places and lost in others

extracts.text: strictly speaking, it is merely the edge of the shade; no pupil in my class being ever allowed to draw an outline, in the ordinary sense. It is pointed out to him, from the first, that Nature relieves one mass, or one tint, against another; but outlines none.
extracts.who: John Ruskin, The Elements of Drawing (Project Gutenberg edition)
extracts.kind: A drawing manual written as three letters to beginners

extracts.text: A dark silhouetted mass is seen against a light sky, the perfect balance of the shapes and the infinite play of lost-and-foundness in the edges giving to this simple structure a richness and beauty effect that is very satisfying.
extracts.who: Harold Speed, The Practice and Science of Drawing (Project Gutenberg edition)
extracts.kind: A drawing manual for art students

questions.onCorrect: Ruskin treats the edge as where one mass or tint meets another, and Speed praises edges that are sharp in some places and lost in others. Together they describe the mixture of hard, soft and lost edges.

choices.label: Draw every edge as a firm, even line round each shape in turn
Leave all edges out, and let the masses simply touch each other
Edges are where masses meet, sharp in places and lost in others
Draw the edges first and shade each mass up to them

misconceptions.feedback: Source A refuses the outline in the ordinary sense, and Source B praises edges that are lost in places.
Source B praises the play of edges and does not drop them, which includes the places where they are sharp.
Source A puts the mass first and the edge as merely the edge of the shade.

questions.prompt: Six edges are described by the values on each side of them. Which is a hard edge, a soft edge and a lost edge?
hints: Compare the values on the two sides of each boundary.
A hard edge is a sudden jump, a soft edge is gradual, and a lost edge has no change.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The black coat and the sunlit rim are hard edges, the turn into the shade and into the core shadow are soft edges, and the dark hair and the grey cat have lost edges.

items.label: A black coat against a white wall
items.explanation: The values are far apart and change at once.

items.label: The turn from the lit cheek into the shade, over a few centimetres
items.explanation: The value changes gradually across a distance.

items.label: Dark hair against a dark background in shadow
items.explanation: The two values match, so the boundary vanishes and the eye completes it.

items.label: The sunlit rim of a vase against a dark curtain
items.explanation: A bright edge against a dark ground jumps in value.

items.label: The soft turn of a sphere into its core shadow
items.explanation: A rounded form changes value gradually as it turns.

items.label: A grey cat sleeping on a grey stone of the same value
items.explanation: With no difference in value the outline cannot be seen.

questions.onCorrect: The kind of edge comes from the values on each side: far apart gives a hard edge, a gradual change gives a soft one, and equal values lose the edge.

questions.prompt: A student presses very hard to make a dark tone, and the paper shines and the tone cannot be adjusted. What does the lesson suggest instead?
hints: Think of the pencil grades and of layers of hatching.
Each layer covers part of what the one before left bare.

acceptedIdeas: A softer pencil, or more layers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A softer pencil, or more layers

questions.onCorrect: A softer pencil or a second layer reaches a dark tone without crushing the paper, and each layer can be adjusted.

choices.label: A harder pencil with the same pressure
A softer pencil, or more layers
A finger to smooth the tone
A heavier line on every edge

misconceptions.feedback: A hard pencil leaves light marks, so it would make the tone paler.
Rubbing smooths the tone and removes its texture and its edges.
Heavy lines are for contact and shadow. They do not give an even dark tone.

questions.prompt: Two oranges have the same hue and the same value, but one looks vivid and the other a grey-brown. Which attribute differs?
hints: Hue is the family and value the lightness.
Ask which attribute runs from grey up to the most vivid form.

acceptedIdeas: Chroma
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chroma

questions.onCorrect: Chroma runs from grey, which has none, to the most vivid colour of a hue, and it is separate from both hue and value.

choices.label: Hue
Value
Temperature
Chroma

misconceptions.feedback: Both are orange, so they share the hue. A hue is the family of the colour.
The question says they share a value. Value is how light or dark an area is.
Temperature is a matter of comparison with neighbours, and it is not one of the three attributes of a colour.

questions.prompt: A student reads that the screen complement of red is cyan, and her painter's wheel says the complement of red is green. Which explanation fits?
hints: A screen adds light and paint subtracts it.
Ask which wheel each answer belongs to.

acceptedIdeas: Screens add light and paint takes it away, so the opposites differ
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Screens add light and paint takes it away, so the opposites differ

questions.onCorrect: Each answer is right on its own wheel. The screen complement is found by subtracting from 255, and the painter's wheel is built on subtractive mixing of pigment.

choices.label: One of the answers is a mistake and should be crossed out of the book
Screens show every colour darker than paint does, so the opposite shifts
Cyan is only a shade of green, so the two answers agree
Screens add light and paint takes it away, so the opposites differ

misconceptions.feedback: Each is correct for its own wheel. The wheels belong to different systems of mixing.
Darkness does not decide the opposite of a hue. The two systems mix in opposite ways.
Cyan is blue-green made by adding green light and blue light, and green is a separate hue.

questions.prompt: A painter has mixed a vivid violet and wants to lower its chroma. Which colour should she add a little of?
hints: Which colour sits opposite violet on the painter's wheel?
A colour mixed with its opposite loses chroma.

acceptedIdeas: A little yellow, its opposite on the wheel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A little yellow, its opposite on the wheel

questions.onCorrect: Mixed in paint, a colour and its opposite give a dull neutral, so a little yellow lowers the chroma of a violet.

choices.label: A little more blue, its neighbour on the wheel
A little yellow, its opposite on the wheel
A little more red, its other neighbour on the wheel

misconceptions.feedback: Blue sits next to violet on the wheel, so adding it shifts the hue and keeps the colour strong. A colour is dulled by its opposite.
Red sits next to violet on the wheel, so adding it shifts the hue and keeps the colour strong. A colour is dulled by its opposite.

questions.prompt: What is the green channel of the complement of (30, 144, 255)?
hints: Take the green channel, 144.
A channel and its complement add to 255.
Subtract 144 from 255.
questions.onCorrect: The complement of a blue is an orange, in which red is strong, green is middling and blue is absent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the green channel of the colour itself. Subtract it from 255.
That is the red channel of the complement. The question asks for green.

questions.prompt: A violet that leans toward red sits beside a violet that leans toward blue. Which of the two looks warmer?
hints: Which of the two leans toward a warm colour, and which toward a cool one?
Ask which of the two leans toward red, and which toward blue.

acceptedIdeas: The violet that leans toward red
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The violet that leans toward red

questions.onCorrect: Red is warm and blue is cool, so the violet that leans toward red is the warmer of the pair.

choices.label: The violet that leans toward blue
The violet that leans toward red

misconceptions.feedback: Blue is a cool colour, so a violet that leans toward it is the cooler of the pair.

questions.prompt: The same grey patch looks bluish on an orange background and slightly warm on a blue one. What explains this?
hints: Think of the strip of grey that runs across all the backgrounds.
Each patch tends to lean toward the complement of its surround.

acceptedIdeas: Each patch is tinted toward the complement of its background
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each patch is tinted toward the complement of its background

questions.onCorrect: Simultaneous contrast makes a colour lean toward the complement of its neighbour, so a colour is never judged on its own.

choices.label: The grey paint is different in each patch of the picture
Orange paint reflects blue light onto the grey patch
The eye is tired from looking at the first patch for so long
Each patch is tinted toward the complement of its background

misconceptions.feedback: The patches are the same. A single strip of grey crosses all the backgrounds and looks different on each.
Nothing reflects onto the patch. The change is in how the eye reads the colours side by side.
Tiredness is not needed to explain it. The effect appears at once when the patches are seen together.

questions.prompt: A painter wants a small patch of orange to glow in a picture that is mostly blue. What should she do?
hints: Orange sits opposite blue on the painter's wheel.
A colour looks stronger beside its complement.

acceptedIdeas: Keep the patch small and set it among the blue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep the patch small and set it among the blue

questions.onCorrect: A colour beside its complement looks stronger. Blue is the complement of orange, so a small orange patch glows among it.

choices.label: Surround the patch with more orange
Keep the patch small and set it among the blue
Dull the orange with grey so that it blends in
Outline the patch in black

misconceptions.feedback: Orange beside orange has nothing to push against, and the patch fades into its neighbours.
Dulling lowers the chroma, and the patch glows less.
A black outline adds value contrast and does nothing for the effect of the complement.

questions.prompt: Warm and cool are judged against a neighbour. In each case below, is the first colour the warmer or the cooler of the pair?
hints: Ask which of the two leans toward red, orange and yellow, and which toward blue and green.
The same colour can be warm in one pair and cool in another.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The yellow-green beside the blue-green, the ochre ground and the red-leaning violet are warmer, and the yellow-green beside orange, the blue-violet shadows and the blue-leaning violet are cooler.

items.label: A yellow-green beside a blue-green
items.explanation: It leans toward yellow, which is warm.

items.label: The same yellow-green beside an orange
items.explanation: Next to a warmer orange it reads as the cooler of the pair.

items.label: Sunlit ground drawn in ochre, beside its blue-violet shadow
items.explanation: Ochre leans toward yellow and orange, and blue-violet leans away.

items.label: Shadows on snow drawn in blue-violet, beside the ochre of sunlit ground
items.explanation: Blue-violet is the cooler of the pair.

items.label: A violet that leans toward red, beside a violet that leans toward blue
items.explanation: It takes some of red's warmth.

items.label: A violet that leans toward blue, beside a violet that leans toward red
items.explanation: It leans toward a cool colour.

questions.onCorrect: Warm and cool are never fixed. Each is a comparison with a neighbour, which is why temperature is judged beside other colours.

questions.prompt: What colour is the screen complement of pure green (0, 255, 0)?
hints: Subtract each channel from 255.
Pure green has full green and no red or blue.

acceptedIdeas: Magenta
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Magenta

questions.onCorrect: (255 − 0, 255 − 255, 255 − 0) is (255, 0, 255), which is magenta: full red and full blue with no green.

choices.label: Cyan, the complement of red
Yellow, the complement of blue
Magenta

misconceptions.feedback: Cyan is (0, 255, 255), which has full green in it. The complement of pure green has no green at all.
Yellow is (255, 255, 0), which also has full green in it, so it cannot be the complement of pure green.

questions.prompt: Which set are the primaries of mixing light, as on a screen?
hints: A screen is made of pixels that glow in three colours.
Ask which set of colours the pixels of a screen glow in.
questions.onCorrect: Light adds, so its primaries are red, green and blue, and each pair gives cyan, magenta or yellow.

misconceptions.feedback: Red, yellow and blue are the primaries of the traditional painter's wheel, and do not describe light.
Cyan, magenta and yellow are the primaries of subtractive mixing, as in printing.
Orange, green and violet are secondary colours of the painter's wheel.

choices.label: Red, yellow and blue
Red, green and blue
Cyan, magenta and yellow
Orange, green and violet

acceptedIdeas: Red, green and blue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Red, green and blue

questions.prompt: A student places a single tree in the exact centre of the picture, with the horizon across the middle. What does the lesson say about that arrangement?
hints: Think about the two commonest faults that the thirds avoid.
Ask what happens to the space on either side of the tree.

acceptedIdeas: It is calm but static, and it wastes the space on both sides
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is calm but static, and it wastes the space on both sides

questions.onCorrect: A subject in the exact centre is calm and static, and half the picture on each side does little. Moving it to a third gives it room, which is why the thirds are a good first guess.

choices.label: It is calm but static, and it wastes the space on both sides
It is the strongest arrangement, since the eye finds it first
It is wrong, since a subject must always sit on a third
It is weak because the tree is too small

misconceptions.feedback: The centre is where the eye goes first, and it is a static choice. The thirds avoid it.
The thirds are a starting point and not a law. A thumbnail decides.
The size of the tree is not the point. A tree of any size in the exact centre is static.

questions.prompt: A student starts a large landscape at full size straight away, and finds that its arrangement is weak when it is nearly finished. What should she have done first?
hints: The first idea is the one already in your head.
Ask what is cheap enough to throw away.

acceptedIdeas: Drawn several small, quick sketches to compare arrangements
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Drawn several small, quick sketches to compare arrangements

questions.onCorrect: Thumbnails cost a few minutes each, and several of them show which arrangement works before the large drawing is started.

choices.label: Drawn the details first, so the arrangement shows up as she goes
Put the focal point in the exact centre of the picture
Drawn several small, quick sketches to compare arrangements
Divided the picture by the golden section exactly before starting

misconceptions.feedback: Details come last. A weak arrangement stays weak under any amount of detail.
The centre is the static choice that the thirds avoid. It does not test any other arrangement.
A grid is a first guess and not a test. Thumbnails are how arrangements are compared.

questions.prompt: A picture is 900 units wide and 600 units tall, measured from the top left. A student wants her focal point at a thirds intersection. Which of these points is one?
hints: The vertical lines are at one third and two thirds of the width.
The horizontal lines are at one third and two thirds of the height.

acceptedIdeas: (600, 200), two thirds across and one third down
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (600, 200), two thirds across and one third down

questions.onCorrect: The thirds lines are at x = 300 and 600 and y = 200 and 400, so (600, 200) is one of the four intersections.

choices.label: (450, 300), the exact centre of the whole picture
(600, 200), two thirds across and one third down
(900, 200), the right edge, a third of the way down
(300, 600), one third across and at the bottom

misconceptions.feedback: That is the exact centre, at half the width and half the height. The thirds avoid it.
That sits on the edge of the picture, and the thirds also avoid a subject jammed against an edge.
The bottom edge is at 600, and a horizontal third line is at 200 or 400.

questions.prompt: On a width of 1000 the golden section falls at about 382 and 618, and the thirds at 333 and 667. A student asks which is better. What does the lesson conclude?
hints: Compare the two sets of lines.
Ask whether the eye can tell a difference of that size.

acceptedIdeas: The eye can hardly tell, so both are starting points
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The eye can hardly tell, so both are starting points

questions.onCorrect: The difference between 333 and 382 is small, so neither grid is shown to be better. Each is a first guess for a thumbnail to test.

choices.label: The golden section, since it has a longer history
The thirds, since the golden lines miss the corners
The golden section, since it is closer to the centre
The eye can hardly tell, so both are starting points

misconceptions.feedback: A long history is not evidence. The lesson says there is none that one works better.
Neither set meets any corner. The two sets of lines lie close together.
Being nearer the centre does not make it better, and the centre is the static place the thirds avoid.

questions.prompt: A house sits at the upper-right third of a picture, and a student adds a road running from the lower-left corner up to it. What does the road do?
hints: The eye travels along lines.
Ask where the road ends.

acceptedIdeas: It carries the eye from the corner to the house
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It carries the eye from the corner to the house

questions.onCorrect: A road that runs to the focal point is a leading line, and without it the small house is easy to miss.

choices.label: It makes the house look larger
It carries the eye from the corner to the house
It moves the house to the centre of the picture
It balances the house with a large pale shape

misconceptions.feedback: The road does not enlarge anything. It gives the eye a path.
The house stays where it was drawn. The road leads to it.
Balance depends on visual weight. The road leads the eye and has little weight of its own.

questions.prompt: How should the rule of thirds be treated?
hints: Is a rule that good pictures break a law?
Think of how many good pictures break the rule.
questions.onCorrect: The grid is a starting point that avoids the two commonest faults, and thumbnails are the test of whether it suits the picture.

misconceptions.feedback: Good compositions often break it, so it cannot be a law.
It applies to any picture with a focal point, not just landscapes.
It gives one guess for where to start, and the thumbnails are how you test it.

choices.label: As a rule that applies only to landscapes
As a law, so that every subject goes on an intersection
As a starting point that a thumbnail can overrule
As a replacement for thumbnails

acceptedIdeas: As a starting point that a thumbnail can overrule
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a starting point that a thumbnail can overrule

questions.prompt: Why does the plan call for six thumbnails and not one?
hints: Think about what you can do with six that you cannot do with one.
The first idea is the one already in your head.

acceptedIdeas: So that the first idea can be compared with others
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: So that the first idea can be compared with others

questions.onCorrect: The first idea is the one already in your head, and it improves by comparison with others.

choices.label: So that one of them is bound to work without changes
So that the first idea can be compared with others
So that the final drawing can be traced from the best one
So that each can be made as detailed as the drawing

misconceptions.feedback: Six arrangements do not guarantee that one is right. They give you something to compare, which a single sketch cannot.
A thumbnail is too small to trace. It settles the arrangement, and the real drawing is made afterwards.
A thumbnail that takes half an hour has become a drawing. They are kept small and fast so that they can be thrown away.

questions.prompt: A picture has a large pale cloud on the left and a small dark boat far to the right. Does it look balanced?
hints: Visual weight depends on size and also on value and detail.
A small dark shape weighs more than a pale one of the same size.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since a small dark shape far out can balance a large pale one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since a small dark shape far out can balance a large pale one

questions.onCorrect: A small dark shape far from the centre can balance a large pale one nearer to it, because balance is a matter of visual weight.

choices.label: No, since the two shapes are not the same size as each other
Yes, since a small dark shape far out can balance a large pale one
No, since a balanced picture has to be symmetrical about its centre
Yes, but only if the boat is made as large as the cloud on the left

misconceptions.feedback: Balance is about visual weight, which is not size alone. A small dark shape can weigh as much as a large pale one.
Symmetry is one way to balance, and a picture balanced without symmetry is livelier.
Making the boat as large would unbalance the picture the other way. Weight can match without size matching.

questions.prompt: A picture has five grey boats and one red boat. What mainly makes the red boat the focal point?
hints: A focal point is made by contrast, detail, colour and position.
Ask which of these the red boat has that the others lack.

acceptedIdeas: It differs in colour from the rest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It differs in colour from the rest

questions.onCorrect: A colour that differs from everything around it pulls the eye first, and contrast, detail and position can pull as well.

choices.label: It differs in colour from the rest
It sits closest to the centre of the picture
It was drawn last, so it is on top
It is the largest, since red is a heavy colour

misconceptions.feedback: The boats are not described by position. The one thing the red boat has that the others lack is its colour.
The order of drawing does not draw the eye. What the viewer sees is the difference in the picture.
Nothing says it is larger. A colour that differs from the rest draws the eye on its own.

questions.prompt: A student plans a picture from thumbnails. In what order should she work?
hints: The choice comes after there is something to choose between.
The final drawing is made once the arrangement is decided.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She chooses the subject, draws six frames, fills each with a five-minute thumbnail, picks the clearest focal point, writes why it works, and only then draws the picture at full size.

items: Choose the subject
Draw six small frames with the proportions of the final picture
Draw a thumbnail in each frame in about five minutes
Choose the thumbnail with the clearest focal point
Write one sentence on why it works
Draw the picture at full size from the chosen thumbnail

questions.onCorrect: The thumbnails come before the choice, and the choice before the large drawing, so a weak arrangement is found while it is still cheap to change.

questions.prompt: A river winds from the bottom of a picture up to a mountain, and the eye follows it there. What do we call a line that carries the eye in this way?
hints: The name says what the line does to the viewer's eye.
It is two words, and the first ends in -ing.
questions.onCorrect: Leading lines work because the eye follows a line, so a road or a river can carry the viewer's attention across the picture.

acceptedIdeas: leading lines
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: leading lines

questions.prompt: A student begins a still life by drawing the highlight on the apple and the handle of the mug in detail. Then she finds that the apple will not fit on the page. What does the lesson say about this?
hints: Each stage assumes that the one before is right.
Ask what it costs to fix an error in the block-in and in a finished detail.

acceptedIdeas: Detail in the wrong place is wasted, so big decisions come first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Detail in the wrong place is wasted, so big decisions come first

questions.onCorrect: An error in the block-in costs a few light lines, and an error under a finished detail costs the detail with it. That is why the order runs from large to small.

choices.label: She should have drawn the edges before the values were put in
Detail is fine, since the page is fixed by the frame of the picture
The highlight should always come last, after every other mark
Detail in the wrong place is wasted, so big decisions come first

misconceptions.feedback: Edges come after values, since an edge is a change in value. The trouble is that detail came before the large shapes.
The page is fixed by the plan, and the plan comes first. Detail drawn in a wrong place is wasted.
The highlight is only one detail. All detail comes last, after the large shapes and values.

questions.prompt: In a one-hour study a student spends thirty-five minutes on the edges of the mug's handle. What does the time plan say?
hints: Edges get about a fifth of the time, and values get the biggest share.
Ask what the plan says to do when a stage's time has run out.

acceptedIdeas: She should have moved on after about twelve minutes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She should have moved on after about twelve minutes

questions.onCorrect: Edges take a fifth of the time, about twelve minutes in an hour. The useful habit is to move on when a stage's time has run out, since the next stage can correct what was left.

choices.label: Nothing, since edges are the last stage and can run on
She should have moved on after about twelve minutes
She should have spent the time on the final check
Edges should get the biggest share, so she was right

misconceptions.feedback: The plan gives each stage its share, and edges get about a fifth. Edges do not take what is left.
The final check is the smallest share of the plan, about a tenth.
The biggest share goes to the values, because they do most to make the study look solid.

questions.prompt: How many minutes of a 45-minute study go to the values?
hints: 40 percent is 0.4.
Take 0.4 of the 45 minutes.
Twice the 9 minutes of a 20 percent stage.
questions.onCorrect: The five stages add up to 4.5 + 9 + 18 + 9 + 4.5 = 45 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage, not the minutes. Take 40 percent of 45.
That is the 20 percent stage. The values take twice that.

questions.prompt: A student's drawing looks right close up, and from across the room the proportions look wrong. What explains it?
hints: When you are close you see the marks, and when you are far you see the shapes.
Ask which kind of error shows up as a shape.

acceptedIdeas: Errors of proportion are errors of shape, which show from afar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Errors of proportion are errors of shape, which show from afar

questions.onCorrect: Errors of proportion and value are errors of shapes, so they appear from a distance, in a mirror, or in a small photograph.

choices.label: Distance makes every drawing look worse than it is
Errors of proportion are errors of shape, which show from afar
The light in the room has changed the values of the paper since she began
Her eyes tire after a long time at the drawing

misconceptions.feedback: Distance shows the shapes. The errors were there already, hidden by looking at marks.
A change of light would affect the whole drawing, and the point is that proportion errors can only be seen from far.
Tiredness is possible, and the step-back habit works even for a rested eye. Distance is what reveals the shapes.

questions.prompt: A student reviews a study whose edges are all hard and even, so that it looks like a cut-out. Which of the six criteria does that lower?
hints: Each criterion names one thing to look at in the finished study.
Ask which one asks for a mix of hard, soft and lost boundaries.

acceptedIdeas: Edges
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Edges

questions.onCorrect: The edges criterion asks for a mix of hard, soft and lost edges, and a study of even hard edges scores low on it.

choices.label: Proportion
Edges
Composition
Process

misconceptions.feedback: Proportion is about the shapes and the ratios between them. Even boundaries do not change those.
Composition is about the arrangement and the path of the eye, and the question is about the kind of edge.
Process is about going from large to small and keeping to time, and the question describes the result.

questions.prompt: Cennini has just called drawing from nature the best guide a painter can have. What habit does he ask for next?
hints: Look for how often he asks, and how much.
Ask what the word 'without fail' tells you about how he means it.

acceptedIdeas: Draw something every day, and enough of it to count
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Draw something every day, and enough of it to count

extracts.text: and with a bold heart you may always trust to it, especially when you begin to have some judgment in design. And continue always, and without fail, to draw something every day, not too little to be enough, and it will do you excellent service.
extracts.who: Cennino Cennini, The Book of the Art (translated by Christiana J. Herringham, 1899)
extracts.when: a treatise from the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century
extracts.kind: A workshop handbook for young painters

questions.onCorrect: Cennini asks for a steady daily habit of enough drawing to be worth doing. The same idea runs through the course's advice to draw short sessions on most days.

choices.label: Draw only when you feel inspired, so the work stays fresh
Draw something every day, and enough of it to count
Draw once a month, at length, so each piece is finished
Draw only from the work of one master, and never from life

misconceptions.feedback: He asks for every day and without fail, whether or not the mood is there.
He asks for a little every day, which rules out rare long sessions.
He has just named drawing from nature as the best guide, and the sentence is about daily practice.

questions.prompt: A study is scored proportion 4, value structure 3, form 5, edges 3, composition 2, process 4. Which criterion has the lowest score?
hints: Find the smallest of the six numbers.
The lowest number is a 2.
questions.onCorrect: Composition scored lowest, so the next sessions should be thumbnails with a clear focal point.

misconceptions.feedback: That criterion scored 4. Look for the smallest of the six numbers.
That criterion scored 3, and another scored lower.
That criterion scored 3, and another scored lower.

acceptedIdeas: Composition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Composition

choices.label: Proportion
Value structure
Composition
Edges

questions.prompt: A still life of a mug and an apple is drawn in five stages. In what order should they be done?
hints: Each stage assumes that the one before is right.
An edge is a change in value, so the values have to be in place first.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She plans first, blocks in the large shapes, lays in the values, works the edges, and checks the whole from a distance last.

items: Plan with thumbnails and boxes
Block in the large shapes and their proportions
Lay in the values as a few flat masses
Work the edges, hard in some places and lost in others
Check the whole from a distance

questions.onCorrect: Every stage rests on the one before it, which is why the work runs from large to small.

questions.prompt: A student holds her drawing up to a mirror and its faults leap out. Why does the mirror help?
hints: A reversed picture looks like a new one.
Ask what the eye has stopped doing.

acceptedIdeas: The reversed picture looks new, so faults of balance and proportion show
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reversed picture looks new, so faults of balance and proportion show

questions.onCorrect: A reversed picture looks new, so the eye reads it as a picture and not as familiar marks, and faults in balance or proportion leap out.

choices.label: The glass makes the colours stronger
The mirror enlarges the drawing so that all the marks show up
The reversed picture looks new, so faults of balance and proportion show
The mirror hides the small errors, so only the large ones remain visible

misconceptions.feedback: A mirror does not strengthen colour. It reverses the picture so that it looks new.
A mirror shows the drawing at the same size. The help is in the reversal.
Nothing is hidden. The picture is seen with fresh eyes, small faults included.

questions.prompt: A student is deciding which boundaries in her still life to keep hard and which to lose where a shadow merges into the dark wall. Which of the five stages of a study is she in?
hints: Think of the order the stages come in, from the plan to the final check.
She is choosing how the boundaries should look once the values are in place.

acceptedIdeas: edges
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: edges

questions.onCorrect: Hard, soft and lost edges are worked after the values are laid in, since an edge is a change in value.

misconceptions.feedback: The values come before this stage. Here she is choosing how the boundaries between those values should look.
The block-in sets the large shapes and proportions lightly, before any thought of the quality of an edge.

flashcards.front: What do we call a drawing of what you know of an object, rather than of what you see?
flashcards.back: A symbol: a stored simplified picture, such as an eye drawn as an almond.

acceptedIdeas: symbol
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: symbol

flashcards.front: What do we call the empty shape around and between objects?
flashcards.back: Negative space: it has an outline and a size, and it has no stored symbol, so drawing it makes you look.

acceptedIdeas: negative space
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: negative space

flashcards.front: Spend ten minutes drawing only the spaces around and between the parts of a chair. Afterwards, rate how closely your drawing matches the chair's proportions, from 1 (far off) to 5 (very close).
flashcards.back: Compare the width and height of the whole chair as a ratio, then the largest space against the seat, since a mismatch in a space shows which part is misplaced.

flashcards.front: What do we call moving the pen over the paper without marking, to rehearse a line before drawing it?
flashcards.back: Ghosting: it puts all the hesitation into the air and leaves one confident stroke on the paper.

acceptedIdeas: ghosting
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ghosting

flashcards.front: What do we call a quick drawing that records the movement and direction of a subject in a few strokes?
flashcards.back: A gesture drawing: it fixes the arrangement of the whole before any detail is added.

acceptedIdeas: gesture
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: gesture

flashcards.front: Make twenty straight lines, each between two dots 15 cm apart, ghosting each one and then drawing it once from the shoulder. Count how many land on both dots and are straight, and rate yourself from 1 (few) to 5 (nearly all twenty).
flashcards.back: A line that is straight and lands on both dots shows that the rehearsed motion and the drawn motion were the same.

flashcards.front: What do we call the ratio of new size to old size, applied to every length of a drawing?
flashcards.back: The scale factor: using one factor for both width and height keeps the shape.

acceptedIdeas: scale factor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: scale factor

flashcards.front: Teachers give different head counts for an adult figure, 7.5 and 8. What do we call such an agreed rule of thumb for proportion?
flashcards.back: A canon: a convention for drawing, since real people vary around it.

acceptedIdeas: canon
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: canon

flashcards.front: Pick an object, measure it with a pencil at arm's length, using the longest side as the unit, and write down the other sides as fractions of it. Draw it, then compare the fractions in your drawing with those you wrote down. Rate how closely they agree, from 1 (far off) to 5 (the same).
flashcards.back: If a fraction in the drawing differs, the part is the wrong size, and a note on the page shows which part to correct.

flashcards.front: What do we call the shorter axis of an ellipse, which shrinks as a circle is seen more edge-on?
flashcards.back: The minor axis: its length is the diameter times the sine of the angle between line of sight and the circle's plane.

acceptedIdeas: minor axis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: minor axis

flashcards.front: The rim of a cup is a straight line at eye level and a circle from straight above. What do we call the smooth curve between the two?
flashcards.back: An ellipse: it keeps the full diameter along its major axis and shortens along its minor axis.

acceptedIdeas: ellipse
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ellipse

flashcards.front: Draw a cylinder from three viewpoints: upright, on its side, and tilted. Check that every ellipse is smooth at both ends and that its short axis lies along the cylinder's axis. Rate each from 1 (neither true) to 5 (both true).
flashcards.back: The axis line through both ellipse centres should run along their short directions in every view.

flashcards.front: On level ground, the farther away an object is, the higher its base sits in the picture. What is this depth cue called?
flashcards.back: Vertical placement: farther bases lie nearer the horizon, so they are drawn higher.

acceptedIdeas: vertical placement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: vertical placement

flashcards.front: What is the name of the cue in which something that covers part of another is read as nearer?
flashcards.back: Overlap: it gives the order of objects but not their distances.

acceptedIdeas: overlap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: overlap

flashcards.front: Draw a landscape in four layers, such as a foreground field, trees, hills and mountains. Give each layer at least two cues: overlap with the layer in front, and then size, placement or haze. Rate how deep the result looks, from 1 (flat) to 5 (very deep).
flashcards.back: If a layer looks flat, check that it overlaps the one in front and that it is paler and smaller than the one before it.

flashcards.front: What do we call the point on the horizon where receding parallel lines appear to meet?
flashcards.back: The vanishing point: it lies on the horizon, since the lines meeting there are level with the viewer's eye.

acceptedIdeas: vanishing point
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: vanishing point

flashcards.front: What do we call the lines that run straight away from you in a drawing and aim at the vanishing point?
flashcards.back: Orthogonals: all the orthogonals of one direction aim at the same vanishing point.

acceptedIdeas: orthogonals
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: orthogonals

flashcards.front: Draw a corridor and four boxes in one-point perspective, with the horizon at your own eye level. Check whether every receding line, extended, meets at one point on the horizon, and rate your drawing from 1 (none do) to 5 (all do).
flashcards.back: Extend each orthogonal with a ruler: a line that misses the point shows which edge to redraw.

flashcards.front: What do we call the compression of a form that points toward the viewer?
flashcards.back: Foreshortening: the drawn length is the length times the cosine of the angle out of the picture plane.

acceptedIdeas: foreshortening
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: foreshortening

flashcards.front: How many vanishing points does a drawing of a tower need when you look steeply up at it and its horizontal edges also recede?
flashcards.back: Three: one for each direction of horizontal edge, and one for the converging vertical edges.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: one for each direction of horizontal edge, and one for the converging vertical edges.

flashcards.front: Draw a house in two-point perspective, with the horizon at your own eye level. Extend its receding edges with a ruler, and rate whether both sets meet at points on the same horizon line, from 1 (neither) to 5 (both).
flashcards.back: Edges that miss their point by more than a few millimetres show which wall to redraw.

flashcards.front: What do we call how light or dark an area is, apart from its hue?
flashcards.back: Value: it carries the structure of a picture, and hue supplies the character.

acceptedIdeas: value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: value

flashcards.front: Of pure red, pure green and pure blue at full intensity, which looks lightest in a grey photograph?
flashcards.back: Green: the eye is most sensitive to green light, so it carries the largest weight.

acceptedIdeas: green
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: green

flashcards.front: Draw a five-step value scale in pencil, with equal steps from white paper to the darkest you can make. Then draw a simple object in three values only. Squint and rate whether the three masses read clearly, from 1 (unclear) to 5 (very clear).
flashcards.back: If two masses blur together when you squint, make the lighter one lighter or the darker one darker.

flashcards.front: What do we call the line on a form where its surface turns from light into shadow?
flashcards.back: The terminator: it curves around a round form, with the core shadow just inside it.

acceptedIdeas: terminator
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: terminator

flashcards.front: On a lit sphere, which band is the darkest, a little way in from the edge on the shadow side?
flashcards.back: The core shadow: reflected light lifts the very edge, so the darkest band lies just inside the terminator.

acceptedIdeas: core shadow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: core shadow

flashcards.front: Draw a sphere in five values with a cast shadow: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow and reflected light. Rate whether the core shadow lies just inside the edge, and whether the reflected light shows, from 1 (neither) to 5 (both clearly).
flashcards.back: The edge on the shadow side should be a little lighter than the band just inside it.

flashcards.front: Lines of width w are drawn at a spacing p. What fraction of the paper do they cover?
flashcards.back: w ÷ p: each repeat of the pattern has one line of width w in a length p.

acceptedIdeas: w ÷ p
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: w ÷ p

flashcards.front: What do we call an edge that fades into the background because its two sides have the same value?
flashcards.back: A lost edge: with no change in value, the boundary disappears and the eye supplies it.

acceptedIdeas: lost edge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: lost edge

flashcards.front: Make a value strip of five squares with hatching, from the lightest tone to the darkest, using spacing and a second layer. Then draw one object with a hard, a soft and a lost edge. Rate how well the tones step evenly and the edges differ, from 1 (poorly) to 5 (very well).
flashcards.back: Even steps come from the spacing and the layers, and edges differ by how quickly the value changes across them.

flashcards.front: What do we call how pure or intense a colour is, from grey up to the most vivid form of its hue?
flashcards.back: Chroma: it is independent of hue, which is the colour's family, and of value, which is its lightness.

acceptedIdeas: chroma
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: chroma

flashcards.front: What is the screen complement of pure red (255, 0, 0)?
flashcards.back: Cyan (0, 255, 255): each channel is subtracted from 255, so a colour and its complement add to white.

acceptedIdeas: cyan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: cyan

flashcards.front: Mix three paint colours from a limited palette. Name each by its hue, its value and its chroma, and say whether it is warm or cool beside its neighbours. Rate how well your description matches what you see, from 1 (not at all) to 5 (exactly).
flashcards.back: Check each attribute separately: squint for value, name the hue family, then ask how close the colour is to grey.

flashcards.front: What do we call a small, quick sketch used to test the arrangement of a picture before the final drawing?
flashcards.back: A thumbnail: a few minutes of work that lets you compare arrangements cheaply.

acceptedIdeas: thumbnail
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: thumbnail

flashcards.front: What do we call the rule that divides a picture into thirds across and down and puts the focal point near where the lines cross?
flashcards.back: The rule of thirds: a first guess that avoids a subject in the exact centre and one jammed against an edge.

acceptedIdeas: rule of thirds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: rule of thirds

flashcards.front: Draw six thumbnails of one scene, five minutes each, then choose the best and write one sentence on why it works. Rate how different the six are and how clear the best one is, from 1 (very similar, unclear) to 5 (very different, clearly better).
flashcards.back: If the six look alike, change the focal point's position, the crop and the horizon each time.

flashcards.front: What do we call the stage in which the large shapes and their proportions are laid down lightly?
flashcards.back: The block-in: its mistakes are cheap to correct because the lines are light and the details are not yet drawn.

acceptedIdeas: block-in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: block-in

flashcards.front: In the usual time plan for a study, which stage gets the biggest share of the time?
flashcards.back: The values: 40 percent, because they do most to make a study look solid.

acceptedIdeas: values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: values

flashcards.front: Complete a one-hour still-life study with a mug, an apple and a cloth in three values, using the stages and the time budget. Score it from 1 to 5 on proportion, value structure, form, edges, composition and process, and write down the lowest one. Rate how honest and useful your scoring was, from 1 (rushed) to 5 (specific).
flashcards.back: Specific notes, such as which edge was too hard, give you a target for the next study.
